I come now to railways, which is a very important matter in so far as the constituency of North Battleford is concerned. Development in Canadian railway facilities during the last fifteen or twenty years has been remarkable. In 1913 the Canadian railways carried approximately twenty-three billion tons of freight one mile; in 1928 they carried approximately forty-one billion tons of freight one mile; in 1930 they carried approximately 29 billion tons of freight one mile; and in 1931 they carried approximately 25 billion tons of freight one mile.
In 1913 the freight carried one mile per mile of line was approximately 800,000 tons, and in 1928 it was well over a billion tons. What does this mean? It means that there has been an increase of 80 per cent in the

The Address-Mr. McIntosh
freight movement between 1913 and 1928. And how did that take place? It was due to the increased technical and mechanical efficiency; heavier ballast; heavier rails; larger cars; more powerful engines; more efficient operation; greater speed of trains by approximately 25 per cent; the increase in the average trainload during the years from 300 to 500 tons; and lastly, it was due to the larger number of tons per load on every car, which was increased from practically 19 to 25.
In so far as the dominion railway problem is concerned, what we need is tonnage. We need freight; we need business, and the only way to get the railways on a sound foundation is to get trade and business and tonnage. How will we do that? We can do it only by paying attention to certain fundamental facts, some of which are to be found in the present policy of the Liberal party. One of those planks is the abolition of unemployment. Another plank in the Liberal program is to liberate external trade, and that can be done only by trading with as many nations as possible, negotiating treaties with countries willing to trade with us on a reciprocal basis; by abolishing the extravagant increases in tariff; by abolishing all unwarranted extra taxes; by substituting stability for uncertainty; by continuing the Liberal policy of the British preference; and by a percentage reduction in existing tariffs rather than a percentage increase against foreign countries in those tariffs. Next we have to liberate internal trade by putting an end to artificial price control and agreements in restraint of trade, and eliminating price fixing in connection with agreements that tend to restrict and hamper trade internally. Internal trade has become honeycombed, enmeshed by secret understandings and agreements. Liberals also firmly believe we can develop trade by putting into every industry the spirit of democracy and by playing fair with both railways.

Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata):	Mr. Speaker, although the well
drafted speeches of the hon. gentlemen who moved and seconded the address have not yet convinced the member for Temiscouata of the soundness of their arguments, let me congratulate them very sincerely upon the correctness of their language. I am sorry that I cannot pay the same compliment to the one who was responsible for the abominable French translation of the speech from the throne. On February 6 I asked a question of the government, as appears on page 301 of Hansard. My question was as follows: May I ask if the government is aware that the French version of the speech from the throne published on January 25, 1934, in an extra of the Canada Gazette, in the Hansard of both houses of parliament and the French dailies, is stuffed with grammatical errors, translation mistakes, nonsense, misconstructions, wrong interpretations, inaccuracies and blunders of all kinds, totalling three score and over.
I was then told by Mr. Speaker to put the question on the order paper. Although I sent a copy to the assistant clerk before six o'clock of that day, it has not as yet appeared upon the order paper. My complete question will include also the following:
2.	Is it the intention of the government to ascertain whether the published French version of this most solemn document of the session reflects on:
(a)	His Excellency the Governor General upon whom has been imposed the task of delivering it in his own name;
(b)	Canadian parliament which under the constitution is bound to give the same consideration to the French as well as to the English language;
(c)	French speaking members of both houses of parliament;
(d)	the whole Canadian community of French origin; and
(e)	the various staffs of official translators?
3.	In the event of that being the case, is it the intention of the government to have the French -translation of the speech from the throne struck out from the said official publications and a proper French version substituted thereto?
I should like to mention one gross mistake which was made not only in construction but

in constitutional law. The first three words put into the mouth of His Excellency by the government are "you are summoned." These are translated into French as "Je vous reunis." Upon page 1225 of the Canada Gazette of December 16 appears the proclamation for the convening of the house. This is signed, not by His Excellency -but by Mr. Coleman, Under Secretary of State. The houses of 'parliament were summoned not by His Excellency, but by the government with the assent of His -Excellency, which is altogether different. In fact, it was not His Excellency who summoned parliament for this session. Time does not permit of my going into the details of this matter. I have brought to the attention of the house the first mistakes which have been made both in the French translation and constitutional law. This proclamation notifying hon. members of the opening of this session is preceded by forty-two notices of bankruptcy but the greatest bankruptcy of all, that which has occurred in the government policy, is not mentioned as such.
Several meetings have been held in the province of Quebec at which were present the three French-speaking ministers with their Tory supporters within the province. One of the favourite arguments put forth is that the members of the opposition have been deliberately wasting the time of the house without offering a single constructive policy to the government.
The speech from the throne contains a paragraph relating to economy which reads:
The accounts of last year will be laid before yo-u. The estimates for the coming year will be submitted at an early date. They have been prepared with a regard for rigid' economy consistent with the requirements of the public service.
I direct -the attention of -the house to Hansard of February 7 of last year -and I hope to have -an opportunity of quoting some of the remarks made by my genial friend, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes). In the speech of that day of the hon. member for Temiscouata there is the following:-
First of all, there are eight vacancies in the Senate. The government have a majority in the Sen-ate, and they are sure to carry their legislation through that body, whenever they think fit. What is the necessity of spending $32,000 per annum in order to fill those vacancies? The government could wait until a time immediately preceding the next general elections, whether they take place this year or next. If they take place this year the government would save $32,000, and if next year, $64,000.
Last year the vacancies in the Senate numbered eight and the saving in salaries was $32,000 less ten per cent, a net saving of

The Address-Mr. Pouliot
$28,800. I congratulate the government upon having accepted a suggestion from the humble member from Tamiscouata. In 1933 the number of vacancies to,tailed fifteen and if the same policy had been followed it would have meant an additional saving of $60,000, less ten per cent, or $54,000 for this session and $82,800, for the two years. On December 30, 1933, seven senators were appointed. Why were these appointments made? Was it because three new Liberal members were to be introduced by the right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) at the first sitting of this house while the government had no newly elected members to introduce? Was it the intention of the government to counterbalance the publicity attending the introduction of three newly elected Liberal members to the house by the appointment of twice as many senators plus one, while there was no urgent necessity for such appointments and while the strictest economy is being preached by the government itself in the speech from the throne.
Another Tory slogan of last summer in the province of Quebec was this:	It was said
by Tory speakers, "At the next election you will have to choose between order, represented by the Prime Minister and his government, and disorder, represented by the C.C.F." The Prime Minister was spoken of as orderly and the C.CjF. and the hon. gentlemen to my left were described as disorderly. I have in my hand some political propaganda which was widely distributed in the Restigouche-Madawaska election. It is rather a screen, and at a joint meeting I showed it to the Tory candidate and told him that if it was a screen it was not wide enough to hide his face and his feet. Here is the quotation, first as it appeared in French:
Un vote pour M. Paul Dube-
He was the Conservative candidate.
-est un vote pour la paix, l'ordre et la prosperite. C'est un vote pour le bon gouverne-ment. II vaut done mieux etre sur le bon cote, celui de la justice, du droit et du maintien de nos traditions.
The translation reads:
A vote for Mr. Paul Dube is a vote for peace, order and prosperity. It is a vote for good government. It is better to be on the right side, that of justice, right and the maintenance of our traditions.

do not vote for the federal Conservative candidate you will get nothing from the provincial government for your roads." It was enough to disqualify that gentleman politically.

In Yamaska the election was between a Conservative and a Liberal, but in the Restigouche-Madawaska election as well as in Mackenzie there was also a C.C.F. candidate. Now, the Tories had repeated throughout the recess that the real issue was between 'the Prime Minister representing order and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) representing disorder. Why then was not the Prime Minister courageous enough to meet the electors of Mackenzie, Yamaska and Restigouche-Madawaska and personally submit to them the thousandth renewal of the unfulfilled promises of 1930? He did not even dare show up in Restigouche-Madawaska, in his own native province of New Brunswick, and this was greatly resented by the electors of that constituency. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) on the other hand was not afraid to speak several times in each constituency-Mackenzie, Yamaska and Restigouche-Madawaska. The Liberal party won the battle on the whole front, and I am particularly glad, as a humble backbencher of the Liberal party, to congratulate warmly the hon. members for Mackenzie, Yamaska and Restigouche-Madawaska on their magnificent victory at the polls. My duty was to give my hearty support to my hon. friend from Restigouche-Madawaska, and I must pay every tribute to the intelligence and patriotism of the electors of his constituency, and to my

own dear friends whom I met during that campaign-. Many of them came from my own neighbouring constituency. The hon. member for Restigouche-M-adawaska is a parliamentarian of seventeen years' experience in the local chamber and he will be a distinct asset to this house.
It is noticeable that a storm of wrath and indignation blows throughout the country from the Atlantic to the Pacific, from Nova Sooti-a to British Columbia. The Canadian people are dissatisfied with the statements of the Prime Minister and the inactivity of the government in so many important matters.
The amendment proposed by my right hon. leader reads:
We respectfully submit to Your .Excellency that Your Excellency's present advisers do not possess the confidence of the country.
I had the honour to accompany my leader, in the beautiful city of Campbellton, where two meetings were held in crowded halls. Turning to the Montreal Star of Friday, October 20, I find an article under the following heading:
King assails agreement to cut wheat acreage. Says Conservative tariff policy strangling trade in speech at Campbellton, JNi.B.-Charges Bennett preelection promises unfulfilled.
My hon. friend from Restigouohe-Mad-awaska spoke, and according to the report:
He charged the Prime Minister with adopting an "I can't" attitude in the face of serious conditions.
The member from Temiscouaita spoke at these two meetings. He spoke very plainly and frankly to the people there, and according to the report he said:
"Competition ever, amalgamation never" had been the cry of Mr. Bennett in regard to the railways when he attained power, said Mr. Pouliot. Mr. Bennett and Mr. E. VV. Beatty, president of the C.P.R. were friends, he continued. He had no objection to their being friends just so long as the friendship did not influence Mr. Bennett. But Mr. Beatty returned from Europe and said, "We must have immigration," and then Mr. Bennett echoed "immigration is badly needed."
Many years ago Mr. Bennett had referred to Mr. Meighen as the gramophone of Mackenzie and Mann. "To-day Mr. Bennett is the gramophone of the C.P.R.", aserted Mr. Pouliot. He declared that if a $60,000,000 guarantee was to be given to the C.P.R., parliament should have been summoned to approve such a guarantee.
The day after, my hon. and genial friend the Minister of Finance also held a meeting. He was fresh from the world economic conference, and I saw in the Citizen of August 28, 1933, that the hon. gentleman anticipated

great benefits from the conference. The heading declares that:
Hon. E. N. Rhodes -feels nations better acquainted.
That is very nice but it does not mean much to the pockets of the Canadian electors. The minister held a meeting in the same city of Campbellton, but he did not hold two meetings-just one, in one hall, and even that was not filled, notwithstanding that he was accompanied by the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. MacLaren), the hon. member for Y-ork-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) and many other distinguished speakers. The city of Campbellton, formerly Conservative, gave a splendid majority to the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska.
At Edmundston on nomination day I was pleased to cross swords with the hon. member for Dorchester, (Mr. Gagnon), who was just back from Yamaska. My speech was very simple. It consisted merely of quotations from Hansard of questions put to the government, which the Prime Minister has always refused to answer. There were questions of special cars to the superintendent of railways, questions on imports of butter, on firms importing butter during the three or four months preceding the 1930 election, and on tax free bonds. I quoted Hansard of last year when the exMinister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) stated to the house that those tax free bonds should be converted. We have a new Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Matthews) whom I congratulate upon his promotion. We remember in the first year he was a member of the house he made a speech about loan conversion, and I hope he will convert his own friends in the government in order that they may convert the tax free bonds so that those who have money shall pay in future. At that meeting the audience blamed and censured the government for hiding the truth from those who have the right to be acquainted with it. What was the result of the election? I was there and noticed the great popularity of the Liberal candidate. Both the C.C.F. and the Tory candidates lost their deposits; the Liberal candidate was indeed very popular, but the verdict of the electorate proved also that the government does not possess any more the confidence of the country.
On Monday of last week, January 29, 1934, as reported in Hansard at page 9, I asked the government whether it was the intention to table the Amulree report on Newfoundland. What was the answer of the Prime Minister? It was the same as he always gives, that it was not proposed to table it; the

My hon. friend-
That is the hon. member for Temiscouata. -has said that Newfoundland means no more to Canada than does some foreign country. I do not think he will have many other members in the house or people in the country who will subscribe to that kind of view. Newfoundland is the odest dominion under the crown. It has been, and quite properly so, one of the boasts of the British people that they have always met their obligations. There has never been a default. When it was open to us in cooperation %vith the mother country, to lend a hand to the oldest dominion, a sister dominion, 1 claim we are entitled to consideration for having come to her assistance under those circumstances. What we did was to say to the banks who came to the assistance of Newfoundland at that time, that we would stand behind them in cooperation with the mother country in ease eventually Newfoundland found it impossible to meet her just obligations. So far from being criticized, I think we have every reason to take credit for having lent that helping hand under those circumstances. I do not need to place it on the ground of patriotic consideration. If, as has been the case in times past, we have come to the assistance of those who have met with disaster in foreign countries, surely we are entitled to come to the assistance of our sister dominion, Newfoundland, in the circumstances.
Is it not beautiful? Naturally this was done, in virtue of the blank cheque policy, as the hon. gentleman said in reply to a question of mine last year. But if I was right last year, why did the Minister of Finance, to use the expression of his own friends, waste the time of the house by censuring me? If on the other hand I was wrong, then why did the Canadian government, at the last world conference at London last summer or immediately thereafter, follow the lines of my humble suggestion? I do not blame the government for having accepted my suggestion, far from it, because millions of dollars have been saved thereby to the Canadian exchequer, but we are highly interested in seeing the Amulree report in order to find out whether it recommends the refund to the Canadian government of the loans guaranteed in favour of Newfoundland.
This is not so bad, but there is something else and I wish to tell the house' that in any speech of mine I have never made a personal attack against any member. On the other hand, there are things which are done by a public man which are related to public matters, especially when a member receives a public grant for something, and in that case we have a right to know to the last cent how it is expended. We are entitled to ask for this and to be told, and such remarks shall not be considered as a personal attack upon any member. Last year I spoke about a second-hand American-made car and I said this:
I have an objection to Canada's coat of arms being on this car. If the car belongs to the country I do not see why the country has bought for the Prime Minister, the apostle of "Canada first," an American made car. If it is privately owned by that gentleman, he has no right to put the coat of arms of Canada on his car.
I am glad to tell the house that the Prime Minister has conceded that this remark was quite right and he has had the coat of arms removed from the radiator of his car. I congratulate him on doing so; it is a step in the right direction. The Minister of Finance at that time said this:
I submit my hon. friend-
He was referring to the hon. member for Temiscouata.

went a little too far when he brought the name of the Prime Minister into the discussion in connection wth a matter which, after all, is his personal and private affair. I say to my hon. friend that the car owned by the Prime Minister was purchased by him in Canada as a second hand car, from a man in needy circumstances who wanted money. I am not going to stress that angle of it, but I know that idea was in the mind of the Prime Minister when he made the purchase. He had to have a car of some sort and he purchased it with his own funds.
That is all right, but I subscribe $400 a year for the upkeep of that car, so I must know whether it is a Canadian or United States make of car. I will not say there is a lack of judgment; English is not my native language, but I will say that it is a misuse of
The Address-Mr. Pouliot

judgment. This is a gentleman who is the protagonist of "Canada first," who says that we must buy Canadian products, and yet he buys a United States made car, and not only that, but a second-hand one. He could have helped his friend by lending him some money on his I.O.U. The question of charity does not come into the matter. Here is an 'American-made car bought by the Prime Minister whose policy is "Canada first." We see that car at the door of the east block every day as an advertisement for American-made goods. How can the Prime Minister speak to-day against purchasing American products? He himself shows that when he says, "My policy is Canada first;" he is not serious, the car that stands there proves the contrary.
I continue to quote my hon. friend the Minister of Finance:
I say I have not the slightest doubt that not only does he give away his $1,800 but much more besides. And when my hon. friend suggests that his only contribution to charity was $250-
Mr. Pouliot: I did not say that.
Mr. Rhodes: I am glad to hear the hon. member say he did not make that statement, because my interpretation of his remarks was that it was his impression the Prime Minister's benefactions were limited to that small sum of money. I am glad the Prime Minister is not here. Even although he may be absent I do not purpose going as far as I might go, but 1 feel obliged to say that the Prime Minister in his generosity towards his fellowmen is second to no man with whom I have ever come in contact in my lifetime. His modesty in connection with his benefactions, which I know to be numerous, is in marked contrast to the character which hon. gentlemen in this house would give him when they accuse him of being a Mussolini and a dictator.
I wonder if Mussolini or any dictator has an American-made car. But my idea was that having been deprived of $400 of my indemnity, and that amount having been given to the Prime Minister, who is much richer than I am, I wanted to know where that money was going. I said he subscribed only $250 in the Ottawa drive. What happened? Three days later he subscribed $500, a hundred dollars more than the tribute I have been forced to give him. A lady wrote me asking me for my contribution and I replied to her saying: My lady, I send you one dollar. My real contribution is $251, because the Prime Minister has subscribed $250 on my behalf.
Now, sir. there is something else that was mentioned in that speech on the 7th of February, and that is the Tokyo legation. I thought it was absurd for the government to build that legation when they were refusing to construct a building for the Supreme Court

of Canada, but were letting the judges sit in a former stable; or to build a new library to preserve the treasures that are in this library, which is not fireproof. But the hon Minister of Finance said: You will get a good explanation when the estimates come before the house. I was not here when the estimates for the Tokyo embassy came before the house, but what did I see in the Ottawa Journal of September 1 last?
Hon. H. Marler Is Financing New Tokyo Legation.
Dominion to repay actual cost, not exceeding $200,000 in ten years at 5 per cent interest.
That is a great bargain-the government can borrow money at four per cent and pay five per cent to Mr. Marler because he builds that legation in Japan. The Minister of Finance had some delightful words about it; he spoke about the patriotism of Mr. Marler -his words will be found at page 2009 of unrevised Hansard of February 7, 1933.

I said that under the blank cheque act it was unfair for the government to supply money to any private concern. Sir, it is too bad that the government did not convene parliament in order to have that matter fully discussed before the house.

It is well, Mr. Speaker, that the
speech from the throne gives the opportunity for discussion of other matters than those referred to in the speech, because there is very little in this speech from the throne that is of any great importance. It is mostly made up of platitudes that do not amount to anything. I am sure that the people of Canada are disappointed that there is not more in it. The old saying is true that hope springs eternal in the human breast, and I am sure that the people of Canada were looking forward to something worth while in the speech from the throne. I believe the government has missed a real opportunity for taking bold steps in the way of reconstructing the economic life of this country. I believe they could have the people of this country with them in almost any steps they might take having for their purpose the improvement of the general condition of the people of Canada. However, there is in the speech no departure from the program that has been followed in the three or four years of the life of this parliament. Not only is the speech itself disappointing, but the speeches made on the address in reply by both the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) have also been disappointing. At perhaps the most serious time in the history of the world they have really talked irrelevancies so far as this debate is concerned. The other day I picked up a book entitled The Liberal Way, in which I read a speech delivered by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). At the beginning of the speech he had this to say:
Never before in the history of mankind has the world known a period of such rapid transition, and of such great unrest, as it is experiencing in these very years.
Despite that fact, and his realization of it, he spent an hour of the time of this house in discussing the question of titles. The Prime Minister chided him for the irrelevancy of his remarks, and then took up an hour and ten minutes discussing the same subject. The people in my constituency are not concerned with titles; there are other things of greater importance with which they
are concerned. A great many of them are concerned as to when they are going to get into employment again. Many of them are concerned with the question of when their sons are going to leave the unemployment camps, and a great many of them are concerned with the question of when their children who have finished their education are going to find something to do. These are some of the questions with which the people in my constituency are concerned, and I have no doubt that this is the general feeling all over the Dominion of Canada.
I do not know that it would be correct to say that my constituents are not concerned in some small degree in the question of titles. There was a rumor abroad that if titles were restored in Canada the Prime Minister might receive a peerage, and that in this case he would leave the country. As far as the people in my constituency are concerned the king's prerogative cannot be exercised too hastily if that can be brought about. If they could do the same thing for the leader of the opposition I believe that would meet with approval also.

speechtext:
Possibly you had the ear of the commissioner. The fact is that I was asked to go in there, and I certainly did not introduce the candidate into the riding; he was selected at a nominating convention that was just as democratic-though perhaps there was less beer

as the convention which nominated the Liberal candidate.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Pretty small politics.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My hon. friend from South Battleford (Mr. Vallance) said that our candidate was hand-picked. My hon. friend ought to be an authority on that, because I understand that he was hand-picked himself, or perhaps it was hand-plucked.
Now let us analyze the situation with regard to the Mackenzie election; I do not think it looks so bad for the C.CF. The leader of the opposition said that Mr. Camp-

bell, the previous member for that riding, was elected with a majority of 3,076. That is quite true, but the right hon. gentleman did not tell the house that there were two Liberal candidates in the last election, and that instead of Mr. Campbell having a majority of 3,076 over the other candidates, he had a minority of 356 votes.
In the by-election of 1933 there were four candidates, the United Front, the Conservative, the Liberal and the C.CF. The Prime Minister made the statement that this was the first time in a generation that the Conservatives had run a candidate in the Mackenzie riding, and the question might be asked why they ran a candidate this time. Perhaps our Liberal friends are not altogether wrong when they say that the former member for Mackenzie was favourable to the Conservative party. At all events they never ran a candidate against him, and consequently we can only assume that he had Conservative support. On that assumption the only reason the Conservative party ran a candidate in this election was to help out the Liberal candidate by taking away from the C.CF. man the Conservative votes that usually went to the Progressive candidate. So my friends should be a little more generous and thank the Conservative party for helping them win the Mackenzie seat.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: We did not run one against you, either.

speechtext:
The Consevatives could not support Stubbs.
Mr. MaoINNIS: They were very much more afraid of Stubbs coming here than were the Liberals, and that was another reason why they wished to help out their Liberal friends.
Now I come to the British Columbia elections, the first major political fight since the organization of the C.C.F. We had no money, we had no breweries, we had no press.

No money?
Mr. MaoINNIS: We had no money. We did not have any. We were confronted with the most unscrupulous and scurrilous campaign that was ever waged in the province of British Columbia. Our Liberal opponents stuck at nothing. The only question they asked was, would it bring votes? If it did, it

The Address-Mr. Maclnnis
was done. Every appeal to fear, every appeal to prejudice, every appeal to passion, every appeal to ignorance that could possibly be made was made by them during that election. Yet despite that, the C.C.F. made a very good showing. The Liberal party received
151.000	votes, about 42 per cent of the total, and they won 34 seats, while the C.C.F. got
115.000	votes, or 33 per cent of the total, but won only 7 seats. All the other candidates combined got a total of about 92,000 votes, or 25 per cent of the votes, and received 6 seats. If the C.C.F. had received seats in proportion to the number of the votes polled, then instead of having 7 seats they would have had considerably over twice that number. We are indeed very well satisfied with the results. We shall be better prepared when the next election takes place, and we are quite satisfied that when that time comes, whether our Liberal and Conservative friends are joined together, as they very soon will be, or are fighting separate campaigns, we shall be able to give them a run for their money.

speechtext: Will j'ou have some money next time?

speechtext:
We do not need it because we have what is more fundamental-we have a policy-and I shall refer to that later on.
Another thing has happened since the election in British Columbia to which I wish to refer. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), during his speaking tour in the prairie provinces, at one of his meetings made a statement that went something like this: You may be hard up now, he said, but at least you are free, but just wait until the C.C.F. gets power, and then you won't have even that. Well, Mr. Speaker, let us see just how free some people in this country are. I am sorry the leader of the opposition is not present at the moment. I should like to have asked him if he had ever lived in a company town or in an employment camp. If he had ever been in any of these places he would have a better understanding of what freedom means and to the extent to which it may be exercised by the workers in this land of freedom. There is a Mackenzie constituency in the province of British Columbia. It takes in some of the company towns on the west coast of the province, Powell River, Ocean Falls and some of those places. This constituency of Mackenzie elected a C.C.F. candidate even if Mackenzie in Saskatchewan did not. And what happened? The managers in this company town of Powell River are now discharging the men in their employ who dared
to exercise the prerogative of their Canadian citizenship by voting for whomsoever they liked. These men voted and worked for the C.C.F. candidate in that constituency-and such action did not meet with the approval of the company so the men are dismissed.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Was there not a secret
ballot there?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
There was a secret ballot, yes, but the names of these men who took part in the C.C.F. organization were not secret, and these men, some of whom have given as long as twenty years faithful service to this company, have been discharged without an hour's notice and replaced by other men brought into Powell River from Vancouver and elsewhere. This is an American company. In those company towns the company is mayor, alderman, laundryman, landlord, boardinghouse keeper, and many other things. In some of these towns it is sufficient for a man to have a labour or socialist paper sent to him through the mail; the post office being on the company's premises, the receipt of that paper, is as good as an order for his dismissal. These companies have received concessions from both Liberal and Conservative governments in the province of British Columbia, but those governments never took the trouble to see that the men working for the companies were protected. The men are not allowed to organize. The government never saw to it that they were given the opportunity to organize into a trade union if they saw fit. And yet our friends talk about liberty.
The leader of the opposition was also very mudh afraid that at some time he might come under the command of the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macpbail) and have to take orders from her. Well, I do not know whether her orders would be any harder than the orders given in a company town by an American company.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is not going very far.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Probably not far enough. There is nothing much that can be done in this house to remedy the conditions I have spoken of, but I hope that when the question is raised in the provincial legislature, as it certainly will be, our Liberal friends will be as liberal in the house as they were before the election.
There is one other matter to which I wish to refer. It is rather strange that it has not been more emphasized during this debate, and that is the guarantee of $60,000,000 to the banks of this country on their advances to
The Address-Mr. Maclnnis

the Canadian Pacific Railway. If I might use an expression that is often used by the Prime Minister in this house, do hon. gentlemen realize the significance of that? Do they really appreciate what it means? Here is the largest commercial organization in the Dominion of Canada, a Canadian institution if you like, with its signs up everywhere that its transportation system spans the globe. Now what does this guarantee mean? It means that this company along with five hundred thousand or more, possibly a million, of the other inhabitants of this country is at present on relief, and the dominion government is dealing with it far more generously than it is dealing with the ordinary person on relief.
The Prime Minister tells us that the security for the loan is good, but the fact remains that the company went to Great Britain to try to raise the money, and they could not raise it there. Why? Because the money lenders in Great Britain did not think their security good enough. They also went to New York to try to raise (the money but the moneylenders in New York would mot make a loan to them. Why? Because their security was not good enough. Then they went to the Canadian banks and the Canadian banks would not loan them money for the same reason. They did not think the company's security was good enough. I wonder if the government, before loaning this money, asked the officials of the Canadian Pacific Railway what they had dome with the profits of the many years of prosperity which they had enjoyed, because we all know that the Canadian Pacific Railway did have some very profitable years. In 1928 this company made a net profit of $51,693,450; in 1929 the net profit was $43,144,543 and in 1930, $38,246,658. The total for the three years was $133,084,651. I think that any company having made such substantial profits for so many years should be able to carry on for more than four years of hard times. The people of this dominion should be careful that they do not take over another bankrupt railway company uipon the same terms as they took over the last one.
There is not very much in the speech to which I desire to refer but there are a few things in it which those of us in this corner have been pressing upon the government for several years. There is the promise of legislation to facilitate the efficient and profitable marketing of live stock and agricultural products. It is very noticeable that no matter what party is in office or, in fact, what party is in opposition, the only policy of any government which is of any value is a policy

looking to the promotion of cooperation. The Labour party in Great Britain was in office in 1931 and they brought forward legislation for the marketing of agricultural products. This entailed the compulsory organization of the producers as well as compulsory marketing. At that time the Conservative opposition opposed the legislation, yet during the last session of the British parliament the Conservative government put substantially the same kind of legislation into effect. The farmers of this country are asking that similar legislation be put into effect here. It has been tried in British Columbia and other provinces but has been declared to be ultra vires the power of provincial governments. The legislation in itself is all right but it does not go far enough, as the farmers will soon find out.
As a matter of fact, the farmers, in asking for legislation of this kind, have arrived at the stage the working men of this country arrived at when they began to organize into trade unions. The farmers have arrived at the trade union stage, if you like. All they are asking for is a closed shop in agriculture. When this legislation came up in the province of British Columbia I was a member of the city council of Vancouver. Every member of that council opposed this legislation except myself. I took the position that I was a member of an organization that had a closed shop and what was good for me, was good for the farmer. Anyway, I felt he was entitled to it if he wanted it, whether or not it was good for him. I think the farmer will soon find out that no matter what legislation is passed, what really matters is the existence of markets. A union is beneficial to a working man only as long as he has a job; the minute he loses his job, a union can do very little for him. The farmer is in the same position. His cooperative organization will be of benefit to him as long as he is able to dispose of the products of his labour but when there is no market, his cooperative organization will not be of much benefit. However, I am sure that hon. members in this corner of the house will give the government every assistance in passing any legislation which will tend to improve the position of the farmers of this country.
The organization of a central bank is also mentioned in the speech. We in this comer of the house have been asking for this for many years. Our Liberal friends tell us that they are in favour of it and have been in favour of it for some considerable time. I believe that is so because I have in my hand a copy of a resolution which was passed at

The Address-Mr. Maclnnis
the great Liberal convention held in Winnipeg in 1917. They were in favour of it at that time but they had nine years in office and did not do anything to give effect to the resolution which they passed. Some of my Liberal friends may have forgotten this resolution, so I should like to put it on record. It reads:
That, in the opinion of this convention, the time has arrived for the reorganization of the banking system of Canada, so as to bring it more nearly within the democratic spirit of proper regulation and control by the people, and with this object in view, be it resolved that:-
1.	The banking system of Canada should be placed under the control and regulation of a banking commission invested with plenary powers in all matters pertaining to banking, currency, coinage and credits, and, in particular power to regulate and control:
(a)	The issues of public currency;
(b)	The coinage of gold and silver;
(c)	The purchase of bullion produced in Canada;
(d)	The amount of call money loaned outside of Canada;
(e)	Interlocking directorates;
(f)	The supervision of credits;
(g)	The capitalization of banks;
(h)	The payments of dividends;
(i)	The relations of subsidiary trust and money-lending concerns to banks;
(j)	And generally, all such matters that are necessarily incident to the proper regulation and control of banking and currency.
2.	Be it further resolved in connection therewith there should be established a national bank of Canada, as a central reserve institution, upon whose board of governors should also sit, amongst others, ex officio, the members of the said banking commission; the objects of said national bank to include inter alia the primary responsibility of marshalling and mobilizing the gold and silver reserves of the nation and the ownership and control of the issues of public and national currency.
That resolution was passed unanimously at the Liberal convention of 1917. During their nine years in office the Bank Act came up for revision, but despite the fact that this resolution had been passed the president of the bankers' association was able to say that all the major amendments which had been made to the act had been sponsored by the association. This matter is coming up this year and I hope our Liberal friends will be a little more articulate in its favour than they were in 1923 when the Bank Act was last up for revision.
The speech from the throne tells us that we are being called together at a time of improving conditions when there are sound reasons to believe that permanent prosperity is near at hand. There may be a slight improvement in the economic condition of the Dominion of Canada, it may be said that throughout the whole world there is a slight 74726-28
improvement in the tempo of production and trade but I do not think there are any signs which would indicate that we are on the way to a return of what we have been pleased to call prosperity.
In the province of British Columbia the unemployment situation this year is very little different to what it was last year. As far as the city of Vancouver itself is concerned, it is costing more this year for unemployment relief than it did last year. For the two weeks ending January 17 there were 8,626 on relief, 184 more than in the previous two weeks, and the cost for these two weeks Was $94,919, while the cost for the comparable two weeks in 1933 was $88,652. Taking the whole province, the situation is not materially better. There was a decrease of little less than 2,000 in the number of those on relief on January 1, 1934, as compared with those on relief on January 1, 1933. So that the situation as far as British Columbia is concerned is certainly not improving at a rate that would lead us to believe that prosperity is just around the corner.
The Prime Minister some little time ago honoured our city with a visit and made the statement that he did not want to leave a bankrupt country for the younger generation. It seems to me that if we do not do something for the younger generation, very shortly the danger will be that we shall leave a bankrupt younger generation to the country. This is the way the situation is developing at the present time.
The seconder of the address (Mr. Barber) in a complimentary way referred to the manner in which the city of Vancouver had dealt with the unemployment situation in the last year. The city of Vancouver has indeed had a difficult situation to deal with ever since the depression began. As pointed out by the hon. member, we have had far more than our share of Canada's unemployed, largely because of the milder climate on the Pacific coast. The city at the beginning of last year was faced with this situation, that it could get no further credit; it could not borrow money, and the banks insisted that it should carry on the activities of the city with such money as could be raised by taxation. We have done so, but those who have borne the brunt of that economy have been the unemployed and the children of the city of Vancouver. The municipal inspector of schools reported at the end of the year that there were four thousand school children in Vancouver in need of dental attention which could not be afforded since the school board was compelled to close the dental department on

The Address-Mr. Neill

March 31. The city of Vancouver has been able to care for its unemployed without further borrowings, but it has done so at the expense of the present and future health of the children of the city. But more than that, although Vancouver is the third largest city in Canada, we had one main library and a branch library, and the branch was closed altogether. The main library was closed for two months of the year, and for the rest of the year was open only during certain hours of the day. I do not think we need look with pride on the administration of affairs if we are going to curtail the cultural activities and those activities that are necessary to the health and well being of the people. There is nothing further I wish to say at this time except to remark again that it is regrettable that this government did not take advantage of this opportunity to bring forward legislation which would undoubtedly have the support not only of the house but of the country at large as well-legislation that would tend to raise the continually depressed and falling standard of living of the great majority of the people in this dominion.

speechtext:
I
propose to use the short time at my disposal in presenting to the house and the government a brief statement of the situation in the coal mining industry, which is one of the largest in the district I represent. I have in my hand the record of output of the coal mines of Vancouver island for the last year. They produced in 1933 601,000 tons as compared with 749,000 tons in 1932, a decrease of 14)8,000 tons. There was a substantial decrease the year before. Of that 148,000 tons of shortage, I can tell where at least 32,000 came from; 22,500 tons were imported from Britain, which should not have been imported, and 9,300 tons came from the United States, which is just about the shortage in the Cumberland mine situated in my district. The shortage there was 36,300 tons.
I obtained the other day a return showing the amount paid by the government under the bonus system they inaugurated a couple of years ago. The quantity on which bonus was paid was this last year 53,904 tons as against 72,284 tons the previous year, and the amount paid in cash, at 50 cents per ton, was this year 826,952 as against $36,132 the year before. That was all for bunker coal, on which the bonus is 50 cents a ton. It will be recalled that the government granted a bonus of $1 a ton for export coal, but I am sorry to say that this last year, as the record shows, no advantage was taken of that. In the previous year there was 600 tons but this year
(Mr. Maclnnis.]
there was none. The Minister of Mines will remember, as I remember, very definite and positive assurances that were held out to us that if this bonus of SI a ton for export trade could be obtained there was little doubt that it would develop into a trade of about 50,000 tons. The responsibility for what has happened lies elsewhere. It is not the fault of the minister, and possibly it is nobody's fault; it may be merely a misfortune. But there is certainly a great difference between expecting to ship 50,000 tons and not shipping any.
In the fall of 1932 I discovered that under the terms of the Ottawa agreements with Britain, coal was being shipped from Great Britain. That coal, I found to my astonishment, was being subsidized by the British government. T do not know and I have not been able to find out the extent, but I have positive knowledge it is subsidized under the Coal Mines Act of Great Britain. It is further subsidized by what might be called ballast rates. That is, ships are coming here to get wheat and lumber under the imperial conference agreements and often, rather than come out in ballast, they take coal at what is practically the same cost. This runs about one-third of what the regular rate would be or what the rate is on the homeward run.
Last year I protested in the house against, this situation and I was told that it was easy to find fault and was asked what remedy I could suggest. I very promptly replied that the remedy was obvious and right in our hands, and that was the imposition of a dumping duty. That was in March, and along about the end of May the government announced that they were going to impose a dumping duty. With that childlike confidence in governments that has handicapped me in my political life, I went home and told my friends that everything was all right; that the government was going to impose a dumping duty. I dhould not have said that; I should have said that they were going to proceed mildly in 'the general direction of considering whether they would or would not do anything. That is what the government did, anyway. I have in my hand a clipping from an Ottawa newspaper, I think the Ottawa Journal, and of course it must be right. The article is headed:
Action is taken to stop dumping bituminous coal. British producers invoiced coal at below market prices.
The article, which is quite a long one, says that the government has been aware of the situation and is going to stop it. It stated that this ooal is being brought out at very low prices and a case is quoted where the

The Address-Mr. Neill
difference between the fair price and the price it was ibeing sold at for export wias something like fen shillings a ton. It was stated that the government was going to charge a dump duty equivalent to the difference between the invoice price and the minimum price in the zone where the coal came from. It was said that this would not yield much revenue but it would have the effect of keeping our British Columbia coal market for British Columbia, which, of course, is desirable.
Later on 'the government issued a circular to their customs agents to the effect that they had reason to believe that coal was being dumped; they gave a list of the minimum zone prices in Britain and suggested that their agents should use that in arriving at the dumping duty. I might explain what the zone system is. The British Coal Mines Act divides Britain into zones and fixes a minimum price under which coal must not be sold in 'the different zones. Mark you, this is a minimum price; they can, if they like, go much higher. This article bears all the impress of being genuine and having been obtained from some authoritative source. In one case the National Revenue office was quoted as being the authority, although I must say in fairness to them, they denied it. At any rate, it was shown in this article that while the minimum zone price was about fourteen shillings a ton, coal was actually being sold at ten shillings for export to Canada and at eighteen shillings for use in Britain. This 'price of ten shillings was, as will be observed, eight shillings below the regular selling price in Britain, but the government did not take any notice of that. One would think that the difference in price would mean a dump of eight shillings a ton, but the government told their agents to use as their guide the minimum prices quoted in Britain and apparently that is about all they did. The best information I have as late as November 9 is that no dumping duty had been applied at that time. I do know, because I was told, that the first 9,637 tons got in free-rather a poor start. Might I say, nothing was done- Perhaps I am not justified in saying that but I oan say this: I do not know and if the question that I asked yesterday is not answered, when shall I ever know?-if the government have power to impose a dumping duty and not reveal the extent of it. This puts one in a very awkward position.
I want to turn for a moment to the question of anthracite. This last year 3,626 tons of anthracite were brought in, valued at $16,929, which works out at $4.68 a ton, or, in other words, the best coal in the world valued at 74726-28J
about $4.70 a ton. Can our friends in Nova Scotia with their bituminous coal mines and we with our deep coal mines compete with that? Further than that, according to the British agreements, the anthracite coal is liable to no regular duty. When I learned that, I said: Well, then, there are various forms of dumping; we will apply under section 6. I said: Why are you not applying section 6? Section 6 is one the minister can apply in order to impose a dumping duty. The answer I received was: Yes, but anthracite coal does not come under that section, because a ruling has been made that anthracite coal is not of a class or kind produced in Canada, and therefore section 6 does not apply. It is very easy to give such rulings, but it is not so easy to justify them. It is not correct to say that anthracite coal is not of a class or kind produced in Canada. That is all that is the matter with that argument and if it is not true, it should not be adduced.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Where is anthracite pro-
' duced in Canada?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
In Alberta at Anthracite,
near Banff. I have before me the records provided by a government department of the production for the last six years. It runs about 900 tons a year; the mine is a small one, I admit. Possibly the demand out there is low or the coal hard to dig, I do not know, but if it suited some manufacturers in the east to say that goods were being produced in Canada, they would not have to produce 900 tons of it; if they produced three dozen, that would suffice. I think I could quote an instance that occurred not long ago where, for the purpose of obtaining a higher tariff, they erected a bogus factory in Canada and produced a few dozen or scores of articles. I submit that a production of 900 tons a year means that anthracite coal is being produced in Canada, and therefore when imported it should be liable to the dumping duty.
Failing in that, I turned to section 43 and I said: At least we have them there. This is a section where the minister, on being convinced that any article is being imported under conditions prejudicial to producers or manufacturers in Canada, can fix any valuation he likes, a fictitious one, of course, and he has often done so, fixing a very high one. I said: We have got them there; but, oh, no, I was then told that according to the British agreement, this section did not apply to anything coming under a British preference, so we were balked again. Therefore the situation is this: anthracite comes in subsidized by the British government, subsidized by a low freight rate which is practically that of ballast,
The Address-Mr. Neill

likely to be reduced still further very shortly, because the steamers are going to be subsidized by the British government, paying no regular duty, no dumping duty although obviously it should be liable as it is produced in Canada, and with no valuation under section 43 because the agreement so states, and this may result in British anthracite flooding our market. It is true that only 4,000 tons were imported last year, but our market is wide open to the British as our defences are down and we have no protection whatever because of the conditions I have mentioned and of cheap labour in the old country.
To turn to bituminous coal again on which the importation is greater under the Ottawa agreements there is a duty of thirty-five cents instead of seventy-five cents a ton which is what we pay when we ship our coal to the country to the south of us. It too is subsidized in just the same way, allowed to use the minimum zone figures instead of the real (price at which it is sold at home, and by low freight rates and all the rest. There can be a dumping duty put on bituminous coal, that is what I am pleading for to-day, and that is what I wanted information about yesterday. They allowed 9,000 tons to come in free which gave them a good start. Let me give an illustration of how vigourous this development is going to be. I have in my hand a number of advertisements of coal:
Best South Yorkshire hard coal, low ash, high heat, order now.
Here is another, a great big thing that must have cost quite a lot of money, making all the standard arguments in its favour, by a company which has all kinds of money behind it, and branches all over the world; if it once gets a footing in the British 'Columbia market it will be very hard to dislodge. It may be said: "Oh well, it is not much after all." But isn't it? It was 1,100 tons the year before and 23,000 last year, an increase of something like 2,200 per cent-rather a substantial increase in these days of declining trade. That is why I am so anxious to find out whether the dumping duty is imposed on this coal, and if not, why not. As I say, the last I heard, in November, was that they were going to get an analysis of the coal. Well, when it is coming in at the rate of 23,000 tons a year, if they just begin to get an analysis, it will be six months before they get around to putting a dumping duty on. Then I asked what amount was paid under this head, and I am told that to give the information would disclose private business. How could it? All I asked was to know the amount of dumping 
duty paid; not paid by Jones, or Smith, or any individual, nor the percentage, but only the amount of dumping duty. The answer could have been $50,000 or 810,000, or it could have been $4 a ton; would that betray the private business of anyone? Would it betray the price at which they bought the coal or the real price in the old country? It would do none of these things; it would be only a record of what the government collected. If the Minister of Public Works lets a contract for a wharf, it is always open to us to ask such particulars, and he always readily and cheerfully answers, telling us not only who got the contract but all the people who bid for it, and whait the detailed estimates were, not only of the man who got the contract, but of the other men who also bid. Any of us can ask for that and get it. Is not information of that kind much more private business than to know whether an aggregation of importers paid dumping duty on this 23,000 tons and if so, what amount? The Prime Minister said he thought it should be given if imported by more than one man; it was, but even if it had been only one it would not reveal his private business. Another point that makes it so objectionable is that it is such a dangerous precedent. Where is it going to end? My friend and I are competitors in the coal business; he cuts prices, I want to know why. I say; I wonder if he is paying dump duty-I know I am. But I have no way to find out. The dumping duty can be put on and taken off, there is no way to find out whether I am getting a square deal or whether he is.
It may be suggested: Oh well, I am playing politics. Nothing of the kind. Several members of the cabinet know that on several occasions I have take action very different from that, when I could have made a lot of political kudos by not dealing directly with them. Here is a telegram which I find in a return I got the other day; it was sent by the secretary of the Mining Association of British Columbia to the Prime Minister:
Coal operators here all of whom are members of this association fear that budget .proposals designed to protect and assist the British Columbia coal industry will not only fail to accomplish that purpose but will have a contrary effect and cause irreparable injury.
Here is a letter from the Hon. N. A. McKenzie, Conservative Minister of Mines in British Columbia at that time. He writes to the Minister of Mines and says:
[DOT]-but I am afraid that the budget's coal policy will injure more than it will benefit the coal business of this province.

The Address-Mr. Neill
He was then a Conservative cabinet minister, so he was not saying it for political effect. That is the way this is regarded out there by men in a position to judge. I am not arguing the merits of the dumping duty system at all; it is often abused and will be again, but we have the system and we are entitled to the benefit of it. We have a high tariff; we have had for some years, and it is alleged by many people in the west that it was imposed simply for the advantage of the eastern manufacturer. I am not saying that, but I say that is often thought and said. If that is the case it peculiarly becomes those who father this tariff, and who support it, to be very careful to see that it is properly and legally applied for the benefit of the natural producers in the west. 'Suppose it had been shirts or shoes coming in; I do not think we should have had to wait until the equivalent of 20,000 tons came before they began to think of taking some action; until a powerful British corporation had got a vested interest started in British Columbia. You know how hard these vested interests kick if there is a proposal to put them out of business; we would have the British government complaining that we were not play^ ing ithe game under the Ottawa agreements. Our right to use the dumping duties is one of those compensating adjustments which the Prime Minister spoke of some years ago, and quite properly so. I would urge that the dumping duty be put on to the full, not playing with some minimum zone thing, but on the difference between the fair price at which it is sold at home and the price it is sold at for export. Remember that as a result of the imperial conference we are compelled in British Columbia to compete with coal which is (1) subsidized by the British government; (2) subsidized by low wages; (3) subsidized by low freight rates, practically ballast rates, and, (4) in the case of anthracite, given the advantage of paying no duty, no dump duty, a price of $4.70 a ton, and no possibility of raising the valuation; and in the case of bituminous, a low duty and the other advantages. We are paying part of the price of the imperial conference agreements. We have lost entirely the coal market that we enjoyed in the United States, just as we lost the lumber market we enjoyed there, not by any deliberate action of the government, but simply by
what one might call the local incidence. I have no doubt that is what the Prime Minister had in mind when he spoke about compensating adjustments.

Well, I don't. There is this

We are entitled to the benefit of the tariff the same as the eastern manufacturer. He is quick to take advantage of a dumping duty; it is within his right, but why should not we? If I have any kick about that it is against the act, not against their action in taking advantage of it. It is there; it is the system we live under; we need it-God knows we need it badly in British Columbia to protect our coal market-and all we ask at the present time is that the government see that the dumping duty is put on. And I might express a mild desire to be told positively that it was put on and to what extent. I urge the government that the immediate and insistent need of the coal industry in British Columbia to-day, besides other remedies, is to have this dumping duty imposed speedily and steadily.

Mr. A. U. G. BURY (East Edmonton) moved the second reading of Bill No. 5, to amend the criminal code (appeals).
Criminal Code-Appeals

He said: Mr. Speaker, I have already explained the purpose of this bill, which proposes two amendments to section 750 of the criminal code, dealing with appeals from summary convictions. The first amendment is for the purpose of providing that an accused person who has been convicted under part XV of the code, and who has been sentenced to a fine, may have the same rights, pending his appeal, as are already provided under the code for persons who have been charged with and convicted of a crime and sentenced to imprisonment without fine or to a fine and, in default of payment, to imprisonment. In either of these latter two cases the accused person oan enter into a recognizance and remain at liberty pending the appeal, but the Strange thing is that a person who has been convicted of an offence for which 'he is sentenced to a fine and not to imprisonment has to pa}' the fine immediately or he may be liable to an order for distress. The purpose of the amendment is to give him the right, pending his appeal, to enter into a recognizance and remain at liberty until his appeal is heard.
The second amendment would preserve to a person Who has been convicted under the summary convictions part of the code the right of appeal notwithstanding that he may not, at the time of his conviction and sentence, have given an unequivocal indication of his intention to appeal. As the law now stands, and it has been settled very well by the cases, if a man is sentenced to a fine and, perhaps without knowing of his right of appeal, pays the fine and costs without giving an unequivocal indication of his intention to appeal, by that act he waives his right of appeal. If later, discovering his right to appeal, within the time provided, he lodges such appeal, he may be met by the crown when the appeal comes on for hearing, with the objection that he has lost his right of appeal. The purpose of the amendment is to preserve such right unless he has given some unequivocal indication that he does not intend to pursue an appeal.
I do not know that I can add anything more. I have the case law here if any hon. member wishes to be persuaded as to the accuracy of my understanding of the law.

Does this
just cover cases of convictions before a magistrate?
Yes, it just covers trials before a magistrate, summary convictions.

Mr. Speaker, personally I see no objection to the two amendments proposed in

the bill now before the house, but when the bill was introduced a few days ago I took occasion to refer it to the law officers of the department, asking them to consider it and let me have a report. I do not think the report is ready as yet; at least I have not received it, and my suggestion is that the bill might be read a second time-because I think in principle it is right-and then allowed to stand in committee until I receive a definite report from the law officers of the department. If that could be done I would be obliged.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset may I extend my congratulations to the hon. gentlemen who moved and seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne. That they performed their duties in a creditable manner was amply evidenced by the hearty response they received from their followers.
For my own part I have felt that in the house this session there is a determination to get down to the very serious problems that are confronting our people in a manner that shows a desire to deal with them in a definite way. I refer particularly to the address of the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) a few days ago, during the course of which he asked for cooperation and the general sympathetic consideration by all members of the house of the problems now facing us. I was in hopes that this sentiment would continue to prevail throughout the session, and I think there has been some evidence that we are making progress in that regard; I believe a determined effort is being made to approach the problems ahead of us with an open mind in an effort to relieve the distressing conditions which exist throughout the country.
I was disappointed, however, when I listened to the speech of the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Thompson), which left the inference with me that the people of eastern Canada felt that they were becoming unduly burdened because of conditions in western Canada. I think that is unfortunate, and I

The Address-Mr. Weir (Macdonald)
hope that spirit is not general throughout the east. After all, many of the people in western Canada are blood relatives and kinsmen to the people in eastern Canada, and it was hoped that a spirit of sympathetic cooperation could continue to exist between the east and the west. I do hope that the sentiments expressed by the hon. gentleman are not generally held in eastern Canada. I think his remarks were very well answered by the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Turnbull) a few nights ago. He gave evidence as to the situation that actually exists in western Canada, so I do not think there should be any doubt as to what the west is actually attempting to do under very trying circumstances.
In that regard, Mr. Speaker, I should like to go a little further and indicate some factors which particularly affect the situation in the west to-day. After all, eastern Canada has gained a great deal from the west and the west has meant a great deal to the east. I think it is well to recall to the house that
many business institutions, financial houses and other organizations which have their head offices in the east depend to a very large extent on the west for their well being. That applies particularly to our banks and other financial institutions as well as most of our manufacturing concerns. In the west we have also a seasonal condition which is very extreme, and which brings about other conditions that are difficult to deal with. This was a new country; it developed rapidly, and that rapid expansion probably has been responsible for the heavy borrowings that have been made. These things will adjust themselves, however, when conditions in western Canada improve.
Just in this regard, so that the picture may be more vividly brought to the minds of hon. members of this house, I should like to refer to a few matters of particular importance to our western provinces. For example, I have before me a statement showing the total value of the field crops by provinces for the years 1928 and 1933:
