Consequently hon. gentlemen will see what western agricultural conditions with reqpect to their main crop have really meant to the western provinces and can realize the effect those conditions have had on the purchasing power of that section of the country.
One could give the figures for live stock. Just in passing I might mention that in Saskatchewan the capital value of live stock in 1932 was $63,000,000, as compared with $146,000,000 in 1928, a reduction of 56 per cent; Alberta $53,000,000 in 1932 and $120,000,000 in 1928, a reduction of 56 per cent; Manitoba, in 1932, $29,900,000, and in 1928 $70,500,000, a reduction of 57 per cent.
Take minerals, to which I shall not refer in detail except to say that, so far as Manitoba is concerned, it is the one bright spot on the horizon. Manitoba's mineral production has increased in value from $4,186,000 in 1928 to $8,714,000 in 1932, an increase of 108-1 per cent. In Ontario there was a reduced value in mineral production of 20-1 per cent. As I say, that is really one of the bright spots so far as Manitoba is concerned.
With respect ito fisheries the value of the fishery products of British Columbia in 1928 was $26,500,000, and in 1932, $9,900,000, a reduction of 62 per cent. Here again Manitoba is particularly interested. We find that the value of her fishery products, which in 1928 was $2,240,000. had gone down in 1932 to $1,204,000, a decrease of 46 per cent. Ontario had a similar reduction. Manitoba and British Columbia depend to a large extent on this product.
Lumber and sawmill products are of importance particularly to British Columbia. We find tblait their value was reduced from $62,500,000 in 1928 to $26,831,000 in 1932, a
decrease of 57 per cent. Here again Manitoba has suffered a considerable loss in the value

The Address-Mr. Weir (Macdonald)
of -these products, falling from $2,045,000 in 1928 to $547,000 in 1932, a reduction of 73 per cent. Consequently, Mr. Speaker, you can realize that the monetary returns from these natural resources of the western provinces have been very materially depleted so that it has -been impossible for them to meet their obligations in the manner in which they were accustomed to do in the past.
Reference has also been made to 'the financial situation of our various provincial governments. It has been suggested that they have been giving too many public services, and that they were unable t-o pay for them. I want to place on record what 'the government of Manitoba has been doing in the last -three yearn.
In 1931-32 the cost of the controllable services in Manitoba was $9,070,000; in 1932-33 $8,218,000; in 1933-34, $6,852,000. The total reduction in controllable expenditures in Manitoba in 1933-34 as compared with 1930 has been 30-1 per cent. I hope the people of eastern Canada will realize that the government of Manitoba, and the same can be said for every provincial government in the west, as well as for the municipalities and other public bodies, has been making a very definite attempt to curtail expenditures just as far as it was humanly possible to do so. When a reduction of 30 per cent in controllable expenditures of any province is made within three years, I think it will be admitted that they are doing their level best to meet the situation with which they are faced. So I would like to disabuse the mind of my hon. friend from Lanark who suggested that western Canada is not attempting to do her part in carrying the obligations which have been placed upon her. Western Canada, if given the opportunity, will come back and will be that great, open market for the products of eastern Canada when times and conditions improve. I hope that our eastern friends will lend a hand in giving the west that sympathetic cooperation which it is entitled to receive as a part of this great dominion.
I wish now to direct my remarks to a few things which were said by my very good friend from Souris (Mr. Willis) in the rough and tumble speech which he made the other evening. He seemed to be particularly concerned over the political designation of some hon. members on this side of the house. Personally I am not very much concerned what I am called so long as I am not called a Tory. I would much prefer to be called a Liberal-Progressive than a Liberal-Conservative. To me the calling of a person a Liberal-Conservative is stretching the point just a little too far. The points of view of Liberals and Con-
servatives are so much in conflict that one wonders why such a title should be maintained. Perhaps my hon. friend from Souris is beginning to realize the ridiculousness of his situation when he attempts to get himself known as a new type of Conservative, as reported in the speech he made a few days ago.
My bon. friend from Souris in his speech the other evening made a very interesting admission, one which I am sure his constituents will not look upon with favour. Referring to tariffs, he said the other evening;
We in western Canada-
I assume he means the Conservatives- -accept the inevitability of protection because we know that in the St. Lawrence basin there is to be found fifty-five per cent of the Canadian population.
I am rather surprised that he should let a slip like that go by. Personally, I do not accept the inevitability of protection, and I propose to use what little influence I have in attempting to show the people of Manitoba just what tariff protection means to them. My hon. friend then harped upon the theme he has been expounding in this house for some time and attempts to prove that tariffs were lower under the Conservative administration than they were under the Liberal. In bo doing he takes the value of goods imported together with the actual amount of duty collected thereon, and from that he tries to establish an average ad valorem rate of duty. He knows his statement is fallacious and misleading to the highest degree.
I have taken the trouble to look up some figures in this regard and I propose to selt them out. The year 1922 was really the last fiscal year in which the policies of the Conservative party were in effect. I find that the total imports for that year were valued at $747,800.000, and the duty collected thereon was-$121,480,000; 1930 was the last year in which Liberal policies were in effect for a full fiscal year. The total imports for that year were valued at $1,248,000,000 and the duty collected was $199,000,000; 1933 is the last fiscal year in which the policies of the present Conservative government were in operation. The total imports for that year were valued at $406,-
200,000	and the duty collected was $77,000,000.
If we deduct the value of alcoholic beverages and the duty collected -thereon, we find that in 1922 the ad valorem rate of duty collected was 15-3 per cent, while in 1930 it was 14-5 per cent. In 1933, we have to add an excise tax of three per cent upon the duty paid value of the goods imported, which brings the ad

The Address-Mr. Weir (Macdonald)
valorem rate for 1933 up to 21-9 per cent. The calculations made by my hon. friend are a bit astray.
In addition, he leaves out many things which he knows should be considered in arriving at a fair calculation of a tariff structure. He knows that there are several factors which should be considered if one is to be fair in this matter. He knows that if a high rate of duty is placed against goods, they are shut out of the country, the only goods that will come in are those classed as luxury goods which pay a comparatively high rate of duty compared to their actual value. He knows also that under our system of ad valorem and specific duties price changes affect materially the amount of customs duties collected as compared with the value of the goods. He reviews a period of declining prices and compared it with a period of rising prices in an effort to make people believe that he was working out a fair average of tariffs.
Let me illustrate what I have in mind. I will take an extreme case, such as 100 tons of steel rails valued at $50 per ton and paying a specific duty of $5 per ton. The value of these goods would be $5,000, the duity collected would be $500 and the ad valorem rate would be ten per cent. But assume that prices have changed and the same 100 tons of rails are valued at $25 per ton, a total value of $2,500. The same specific rate applies. The duty collected is still $500 but the ad valorem rate has increased to 20 per cent. I assume my hon. friend would say that this represents an increase of 100 per cent in the tariff. He did not take into consideration the period of great industrial expansion which we had during the war when a large amount of raw material came into the country at a very low rate of duty or free of duty and was later reexported. My contention is that it is impossible to compare the ad valorem rates of duty on goods coming into this country at any particular time with the rate on goods coming in at another time.
I should like to give the actual tariff rates which applied on certain classes of goods which are of particular interest to western Canada as a whole and to the people in the constituency of my hon. friend as well. For example, take mowers, binders, reapers, cultivators, harrows, horse-rakes, seed drills, manure spreaders and weeders. In 1921 the British preferential rate on this item was 124 per cent; the intermediate rate was 124 per cent and the general 124 per cent. In 1930 the British preferential rate was free, the intermediate was 6 per cent and the general 6 per cent. In 1933, the British preferential was
still free, but very little if any of this class of goods is brought in from Great Britain. In that year the intermediate rate was 15 per cent and the general, 25 per cent. The greater proportion of these goods come under the general rate. The same thing applies to plows and threshing machines. In 1921 the British preferential rate on this item was 12J per cent; the intermediate, 17J per cent and the general, 174 per cent. In 1930 the rates were free, 10 per cent and 10 per cent and in 1933, free, 15 per cent and 25 per cent. The same thing applies to nearly all other classes of farm machinery brought into the country. In the case of spraying machines, fruit and vegetable grading machines, pruning hooks and pruning shears, in 1921 the British preferential rate was 124 per cent, the intermediate 20 per cent and the general 20 per cent. In 1930, the rates were free, 10 per cent and 10 per cent respectively while in 1933 they were free, 15 per cent and 25 per cent. In the case of well drilling machinery of a kind not manufactured in Canada, the rates for 1921 were 15 per cent British preferential, 25 per cent under the intermediate and 274 per cent under the general. In 1930 the rates were free across the board. In the case of machinery for concentration of ores, in 1921 the British preferential rate was 15 per cent; intermediate, 25 per cent and general, 274 per cent, while in 1930 the rates were 10 per cent, 15 per cent and 20 per cent respectively. Mine hoists, of a class not made in Canada: in 1921 the British preferential rate was 15 per cent; intermediate, 25 per cent, and general 274 per cent, while in 1930 the rates were free, 5 per cent and 10 per cent respectively. In 1921 the rates on engines for fishermen's boats were British preferential, 15 per cent; intermediate, 25 per cent and general 274 per cent; in 1930 under the British preference they were free; under the intermediate tariff 124 per cent and under ttihe general 15; and in 1933 the figures were free, 124 per cent and 15 per cent. I could enumerate a large number of others. Hon gentlemen will recall that a duty of 25 per cent was placed on cream separators and 10 per cent on barbed wire. I do not think therefore that my hon. friend's tariff averages will amount to much when he tells the people the tariffs that have been imposed specifically on the various articles in the tariff schedule, particularly those affecting the farmers of western Canada. That is my point. The averages do not signify anything but merely confuse the whole issue so that people do not thoroughly understand it. One should at all times give the actual rate of duty if one wishes to be
442	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Weir (Macdonald)
fair in this regard. I should certainly expect that the hon. gentleman would be just as much interested in making it possible for the farmers of the west to receive their goods at as low a cost as possible, instead of accepting the inevitability of protection. I suppose he means by that that he is not going to labour the matter very much inasmuch as he realizes the preponderance of population in eastern Canada to be the determining factor in such matters. For this reason he is going to be content to let the inevitable continue. Personally I am not going to take that position; I refuse to accept the inevitability of protection in this regard. I propose to use all the influence I have to bring about a reduction in tariffs. Surely the hon. gentleman must realize that even his leader admitted the injustice of the tariff when he introduced the five cents per bushel bonus on wheat, describing it as a compensating adjustment for western agriculture. Instead of accepting the inevitability of protection with respect to tariffs; he should take his place alongside the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Stitt), who made a courageous speech in this house the other afternoon, he would then be making a real contribution to the house and to the country.
I wish now to direct my remarks to the wheat agreement. I view this agreement a little differently to the way in which some hon. gentlemen in this house regard it.
I do not think anyone likes the agreement;
I do not think that even the government likes it. I do not see how any person in Canada can view with favour a reduction in wheat acreage. More than that, in my opinion it does not matter whether the agreement is made effective or not; natural causes will carry out the purpose of the agreement whether it is adopted or not. Moreover I cannot see that we are going to be able at the rate of shipments to-day to come up to the quota allowed under the agreement this year, namely, 200 million bushels, without forcing sales and thereby depression prices. So far no machinery has been set up to handle it, and apparently it will be left to take care of itself, so that we shall still have a large carryover next year. In 1934-35 we are to have a quota of 15 per cent less than the average of 1931-33, which is estimated to give us a quota of from 263 million to 294 million bushels. I still feel that we shall have difficulty, in shipping this quantity of grain even in that crop year. So that we are likely to arrive at the end of 1935 still holding a considerable quantity of wheat.
I doubt whether the quota system so far suggested can be worked back to the farmer,

and if an attempt is made to carry it out it will require a terrific amount of supervision to carry it out. On the other hand, if I could be convinced that this wheat agreement would be lived up to, not only to the letter but in the spirit, by all the countries subscribing to it, and if it could be demonstrated to be a step towards a genuine form of international cooperation, then I think that Canada should play her part in the matter. But I do think that the machinery so far suggested is not sufficient to carry out the agreement. It seems to me that it will be unfair to the producers if an attempt is made to carry it out without some additional machinery in the form of a national marketing organization. Suppose we come to the end of the crop year 1935, when the agreement expires, and our own crop is going on the market. We might have a big crop in this country and the tendency might be to keep prices down. If it were found later on, through the working of the agreement or otherwise, that the world's surplus of wheat had been considerably reduced, with the resulting increased prices later on, we should find this situation then, that the farmer would be delivering grain in the fall at low prices while someone else would be getting the advantage of the later increase. The same thing happened in connection with the London agreement with respect to hogs this fall. I saw many farmers last fall delivering hogs at 4 and 5 cents per pound, only to find when the agreement became more effective, hogs increased in price to almost 9 cents per pound on the Winnipeg market. It is hardly fair to place one class of people in a preferred position, leaving another class subject to the ordinary fluctuations of prices when normal conditions do not prevail.
There are several other factors in regard to which I think it is particularly necessary for us to have information before the agreement is implemented. For instance, I should like to know on what basis the figures have been calculated as affecting other countries entering into this agreement. I think it is also essential to know just what the situation is as regards rye. Wheat and rye go together so far as the old country production is concerned. I am told that the rye production in the European countries has been materially reduced at the expense of wheat. Now, if they reduce wheat, what will they do with rye? In my own province there is durum wheat to be taken into account. I presume it is included in the total amount contemplated in the agreement. Durum is used for different purposes. I am told that the Italian

The Address-Mr. Weir (Macdonald)
people in particular are making very high class macaroni and spaghetti products out of our durum wheat, whereas our Canadian manufacturers of similar products are continuing to use our ordinary wheat.
The other day the Prime Minister showed to the house a poster from France indicating, that the French people were attempting to carry out the spirit of the wheat agreement.
I am prepared to accept that. I also saw that poster some time ago and I am told that in addition to placing that poster in all the post offices throughout France, the FVench have enacted legislation whereby they will penalize any farmer who breaks up any new land and sows it to wheat. If that step has been taken with the idea of carrying out the spirit of the agreement, well and good, but we should watch very closely to see whether that is the situation. I accept in good faith the propaganda they are putting out, but we all know the people of France are to-day beginning to protest against the high taxes they are paying because of the high duties imposed on wheat, so that these matters must be watched carefully.
There are other matters that should be kept in mind in the carrying out of this agreement. It is not sufficient to let it work alone; we should at all times be endeavouring to find new uses for wheat. I am told on good authority that, for example, in this country 35,000,000 bushels of wheat are being fed to poultry. One can hardly realize that such a quantity could be used for that purpose. There must be other uses to which wheat can be put and may I say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) that a very definite effort should be made to popularize the use of wheat throughout the world. Other concerns who are using other kinds of food products put on extensive advertising campaigns to demonstrate new uses for the different products they have, yet I have failed to see any definite or constructive effort to sell wheat or to popularize it in other countries or even in this. Would the General Motors company be content simply to send its automobiles and trucks over to Liverpool or some other market and leave them in a warehouse there hoping the people would come in and buy them? Certainly not. We must get a definite, active campaign started to popularize the use of wheat and make everybody eat just as much of it as possible.
I wish to repeat that if an attempt is going to be made to carry out the wheat agreement there must be added to it or made a part of it some form of national marketing organization. I would hate to see the marketing of
grain left to a wide open speculative system and the farmer subjected to the abuses that might follow it. I know it will be difficult to carry it out; I am afraid the situation at the present time is such that there may be a disposition at least on the part of some, because of what has been happening, to increase rather than to decrease their acreage. On the other band, however, I feel that at least for this year it is not going to be necessary actually to set up any machinery to carry out the wheat agreement, the simple reason being that natural causes such as drought, grasshoppers, lack of feed and lack of power to put in a crop, will reduce the acreage to the desired extent.
Reference is made in the speech from the throne to the creation of a central bank, all parties being agreed on such a policy. I do not in any sense feel competent to deal with a matter of this kind, but there are two points that stand out strongly in my mind with regard to it. In the first place, if our monetary policy has such a vital effect on the livelihood and welfare of the people, it seems logical that our currency should be nationally controlled. Secondly, with all the ramifications and the sad experiences that Canlada has had in the field of international exchange in the last few years, it would seem proper that we should have a national bank to speak for all of Canada, with respect to international monetary affairs. I feel, however, some people have received a wrong impression on what a central bank will do; there are some who think that simply by the establishment of a central bank, credit will be easier for them. That is not the case. A central bank, government owned, will have to conduct its banking business on just as sound a basis 'as our private banks have done in the past. The creation of a central bank will not make interest rates any easier for the 'ordinary individual, and as long as government and other public bodies continue to pay high raltes of interest, just so long will the individual have to do likewise.
Another important matter that arises in connection with our banks is this: many directors are also directors of other corporations. I am just wondering if the ordinary individual reoeives the same consideration as that accorded to these other corporations. It is important that that point should be brought forward. Further, the inference has gone abroad that the lack of bank accommodation, particularly to farmers, has been because of heavy losses that those institutions have taken in the agricultural business. In the revision
The Address-Mr. Fournier

of these 'bank charters the situation, with respect to bank losses should be definitely brought out because I doubt very much whether their losses have been sustained in the agricultural business.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very
pleased, indeed, at the outset of my remarks on the address, to have the opportunity of extending my sincere congratulations to the three members elected since the last session. If we glance over the various sections of this country, we note that the people seem to be unanimous in censuring the policy of this government. In Saskatchewan, the 'Conservatives have almost been entirely wiped out; in the constituency of Mackenzie, the party to my left has been crushed and a Liberal has been elected by an almost incredible majority, in Quebec, the Yamaska election gave the same result; in the Maritime provinces, the Liberal candidate carried Restigouche-Mada-waska by almost an incredible majority. This seems to be a harbinger of the people's feelings. The nation which had no opportunity, previous to these three elections, to express its wishes, has just given its verdict which condemns without a shadow of doubt the party in office, and in my opinion, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) should in the near future appeal to the people. The members elected have always been Liberal, are highly gifted and appreciated by their constituency; I, therefore, associate myself with all in extending to them our sincere congratulations and our wishes for a brilliant career in the house.
Undoubtedly there exists a crisis the like of which has never been felt for a number of centuries. It is world wide and no country can boast of having escaped its consequences. We are passing through an era of change and evolution and all nations harbour in their midst, to-day, a restless element, dissatisfied with their lot, wondering whether to continue the capitalist system or adopt new ideas. In Europe, various nations have discontinued the parliamentary system to adopt either fascism of nazism or bolshevism or again other forms of government unknown in America. Within a year the United States themselves, without entirely doing away with the capitalist system, have thought fit to change it so as to give to the state a greater control over the economic life of the country, a control extending to trade, industry and to all other fields of national activity. In this country we have continued our

capitalist system without change. In my opinion, it is still the best for a young country like ours, considering its relative situation; however, I admit, with many others, that the abuses of this system are responsible for the present state of things.
Undoubtedly, Canada like all other countries, suffers from depression and unemployment. All admit that we have unemployment. Perhaps, we disagree sometimes as to its spread; we certainly do not agree as to the remedies to apply in order to relieve the situation. Within the last three years, unemployment has certainly spread in our country. The only remedies have consisted in government loans, new taxation, in money expended on public works, contributions to distressed provinces or doles.
Public works were the first which the government endeavoured to apply, all know with what success. It was an exceedingly expensive method. Proportionately it gave the least results for the money expended in order to relieve unemployment. This method was dropped by the government in order to adopt purely and simply the dole system and charitable means.
To-day, the dominion, provincial and municipal governments carry on the dole systems, giving from hand to hand to those in distress. However, this system has very little improved the situation of those who are in want. I have but to point, as an example, to the city I represent to prove that, notwithstanding the large amounts expended in our midst to relieve distress, we are, more than ever, faced with unemployment and poverty. At the 1931 session, 2,000 persons, in Hull, were depending on government assistance. The number has increased to 6,500 within three years. Notwithstanding public works carried out, the number of unemployed has increased and will continue to do so, unless a remedy is found to bring new life to industries which give work to our people.
At present, in the city of Hull, with a population of 29,000 souls, we support 6,500 persons, at a cost of $30,000 per month, supplied by the Dominion and provincial governments and one-third by the municipality. We have no choice, we >must make a loan of nearly $600,000 to meet the outlay necessitated by unemployment, public works and the funding of our floating debt. And I must confess that, at the last projected public sale of properties, the list comprised 841 properties to be sold for municipal taxes. This does not include vacant lots but only

The Address-Mr. Fournier
houses. We have reached the point where certain property holders prefer demolishing their houses than pay their taxes or run the risk of having to pay higher taxes.
Do not imagine that I blame this government alone for such a state of things. The situation existing in Hull, is that, I think, of all other cities in the Dominion. It is the result of many past events, it is the consequence, probably, of the inconsiderate increase of the national debt, of our shortcomings, and I think it would be ridiculous to blame one man or a party for what we are reaping to-day. However, I believe that the party in office has not put into practice any policy which might relieve the situation or uproot the evil.
So far as unemployment, suggestions were made by both the Liberal party and the party to my left. The government did not follow these suggestions and has not succeeded in improving the situation. Why this obstinacy in refusing to appoint a federal commission, comprising the representatives of all public corporations, who are familiar with the conditions existing throughout the country, so as to cooperate with the Dominion, provincial and municipal governments in the distribution of relief, the methods to be adopted to find work for those who are unemployed and thereby improve the lot of those in distress?
As a permanent measure, the enactment of an unemployment insurance was often suggested. This unemployment insurance scheme has not been carried out or been considered! or even communicated to the house, as a measure, by the government. It is, perhaps, difficult to put it into practice at a time of crisis. However, if we delay too long and prosperity returns, we shall soon have forgotten our present hardships and we shall pigeon-hole a measure which should be enacted in a country which seeks progress, in a young country like ours and which may become very prosperous.
The present act to relieve unemployment contains provisions in connection with the back-to-the land movement. This scheme can certainly be very helpful to those who, in our cities, depend, to-day, on the dole. Again, this evening I came across a last year's report on the subject. In Ontario, 329 families, comprising 1,763 persons were settled by the government on lands in New Ontario. Those who do not yet suffer from the get-rich-quick ailment-an ailment which seems to have spread in certain sections of our country -those who have sufficient courage to forsake
city life so as to settle on new lands, will certainly find there, a home, fuel and food.
If it be not a luxurious life, it is certainly a healthy one, the one our forebears were familiar with and which gave them the means of raising large healthy and bright families.
I am aware that it is difficult to persuade a great number of city folks to give up the easy city life to settle on lands and undergo the hardships of a settler; however, I think that the government, through advertising and giving greater assistance to those who wish to settle on lands, should endeavour to increase the number of those who are happy in the country. In Quebec, it seems that this return to-the-land movement is the one which benefits most of the people.
I, therefore, congratulate the government for having thought of setting aside an amount for the back-to-the-land scheme. However,
I request the government to decrease, if not to completely eliminate the quota which municipalities must furnish in the settlement of these families.
The financial situation of towns in Quebec -I am not acquainted with the situation of towns outside of this province-is such that our municipal councils find it impossible, at present, to furnish one-third of the amount required to settle these people on farms. Both Dominion and provincial governments should, in my humble opinion, share the cost of settling these people. Colonization is not within the piu-view of municipalities, but of provincial and Dominion governments. Why then not unburden the municipalities of this weight, when they are almost faced with bankruptcy? I feel certain that the people of 'Canada would be grateful to the federal and provincial governments, if such a measure were enacted.
May I now refer to our trade. I shall not quote any figures, as numerous speakers who have preceded me have done so in their speeches. Statistics have their importance; however, it is said that they can be twisted as one wishes. I prefer expressing the views of the people, with whom we come in contact daily, in connection with the present situation, the way the country is managed and what is expected from our legislators. There is no doubt that, in value, our trade imports and exports have decreased by half. No one denies that. As to the figures, the Bureau of Statistics proves it beyond doubt. Has it decreased in the same proportion as to volume? Without quoting figures, I think the ratio is the same. If not, how explain the

The Address-Mr. Bouchard
considerable deficits of our transportation systems, either by water or railway? If the same quantity of goods had been carried during these last years, no doubt the revenues of our transportation systems would have been larger than they are. To Liberals and serious people, the cause of these deficits is necessarily to be found in the fact that the present tariffs have hindered the expansion of our trade abroad. Reciprocity was discussed last year; I trust that the government this year will negotiate such a treaty with the United States.
I have, sir, in my few remarks, endeavoured to express my views on present conditions. We take a great interest in all these problems and I trust this government will take the necessary measures to bring back prosperity to this country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to say a few words before this largely depopulated house at this late hour of this parliamentary week it occurs to me to remark upon the fact that the government this year could not draw upon newly elected members in choosing the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Of course that is due to no mere whim of fate but rather to a decided expression of the opinion of the public at large. The government should not forget the old saying, after the three elections that have been lost, that three is a crowd. We all expect that the day will soon come when this will be demonstrated.
Both the mover (Mr. Gofoeil) and the seconder (Mr. Barber) of the motion have acquitted themselves well, and what they lack in ingenuousness they make up, perhaps, in political ability. They have demonstrated, it is true, a youthful faith in the policies of their government, a faith, however, which is not in keeping with the thought of the people at large.
My congratulations naturally go to the three newly-elected members. They have championed the rights of the people; they have championed Liberal thought, and they were all elected by large majorities, which is a sign of the times. The enticements of the spider which succeeds in catching the fly in its web are nothing in comparison with the enticing promises that were made during the last election to induce the people to vote for 
the Conservatives. Statesmen in these times I know are not sleeping on beds of roses. But instead of trying to apply some permanent cure to our diseases it seems to me they merely resort to all sorts of expedients, they are like a little boy playing with a yo-yo, drawing taxes up and letting them out again. The palliatives applied by the administration have accentuated the disease instead of curing it, and indeed no serious effort has been made to remedy the situation. The country is entitled to something more than mere palliatives. Those who have gained power through extravagant promises should not be surprised at evidence of an extravagant distrust on the part of the people.
I do not propose to deal at any great length, Mr. Speaker, with the different proposals contained in the speech from the throne. I shall not give any figures; as a matter of fact I think they have all been given. With his usual mastery of facts my right hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King) has dealt with this question in a very illuminating way, so much so that he has silenced my hon. friends opposite. The speech from the throne, in common with the four previous speeches, is a masterpiece of illusive statements and evasive hopes. The popular mind cannot be changed at once by glowing prophecies of instant recovery, without some more substantial evidence being offered. The supreme efforts of the government in its dying days-I hope-will not revive the public confidence so widely shaken by nearly four years of inefficient administration.
Perhaps you will agree with me, Mr. Speaker, when I state that the economic depression has brought about a greater intellectual ferment, with a natural desire for new ideas and a greater disposition towards the exchange of views. Unfortunately these new suggestions have not gained the support of the government benches, where a lack of cooperation is obvious. In their public utterances hon. gentlemen opposite charge us with a lack of cooperation, as though the official opposition were in power. Well, we are here to offer our suggestions and it is up to the government to put them into effect. With no desire to claim credit for a panoramic mind or a quack cure-all remedy I wish to express a few reflections at random, such as might be uttered by a habitant looking

The Address-Mr. Bouchard
over his country. Coming from the province with the highest proportion of spinning wheels and the smallest- proportion of steering wheels I am bound to be rated as a traditional, not to say a fossilized, old-fashioned type, but it is clear to me that having regard to the impulse of industrial, commercial and financial forces the world today is a world in compartments, more mechanical than thoughtful. An attempt has been made to build sky-high a great industrial tower, a Babel, which has brought about a confusion of languages, and in all this turmoil the dominating voice is that of the bankers, who form a kind of moneyarchy. In this period of turmoil, which has been accentuated by this government, the financial man is speaking one language, the farmer another and the labouring man another, and with the present government in power there is very little hope for any complete understanding.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that it is the duty of public spirited men to offer their contributions when the ship of state is struggling against a heavy sea. It is not only for the crew but also for the passengers-or the back benchers-to lend a helping hand. Unless capitalism, which is no evil in itself, is rationalized, socialized, humanized and ruralized we do not know where the ship of state will land. What I claim for agriculture is not for mere class advantage but for the good of the country. During this present crisis the farmers have given the world an example of fecundity, perseverance and endurance, but with the policies of this government complicating the situation the future is very cloudy. By increasing the tariff this government has increased the price of practically every commodity the farmer has to buy and has made it more and more difficult for the farmer to trade with the world. The tariff on cream separators, barbed wire, fertilizer, cotton goods and so many other commodities has not been put there to help the farmer. A government which allows manufacturers to pile up dividends in the face of farmers putting in long hours of labour on the land should not be surprised at the results of the recent by-elections.
The other day when the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) was so ably winding up the debate on his motion for shorter hours of labour I was reflecting on the force of his arguments, which were not less convincing than those advanced by the hon.
member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan). I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that shorter hours are bound to come with the ever increasing efficiency of machinery, but this is only one feature, and it should be interwoven with a scheme which at the same time would afford similar advantages to the workers on the soil. Let us get all the protection possible for the manufacturers, also all possible advantages for the labour men, such as shorter hours, a minimum wage, unemployment insurance, and so on. To all these policies I do not object at all, but if, while the government is applying these policies, the farmer is neglected by the government as he is at the present time, the evils from which we are suffering will only be increased. Today the farmer is over-neglected and the manufacturer is over-protected, and what is the final result? The present crisis, I submit, is more than anything else a question of unemployment, and unemployment is a result, more than anything else, of a disinclination to the land. But what is worse, this government, not satisfied with having plagued the farmer with high tariffs, taxes on sugar and postage stamps, sales taxes and so on, is asking the farmer to pay for that for which he is not responsible.
I think you will agree with me, Mr. Speaker, that unemployment is a by-product of industry, and now the government is turning to the farmer and asking him to pay his share of the unemployment in industry. Professor H. E. Armstrong writes in the Sunday Times of recent date:
We have too long made manufacturing industry the prime object of our national being. We have largely sold man's birthright, agriculture, for no mere mess of potage, but for mechanisms with which we can accomplish almost anything that we desire to do, even to the extent of making ourselves all but unnecessary. We call this rationalization. .Nothing less rational could well be.
We have deprived the farmer of his markets by our excessive tariffs and are now asking him to pay a large Share of the taxation to cure unemployment. But that is not all. While the government of my province has spent up to the end of the year 1932 over $150,000 in premiums to the farmers to help them buy fertilizer, at the same time this government imposes a tax in the form of a tariff on the fertilizer which the farmer uses when it enters this country manufactured. I agree with Professor Albert Einstein who,

The Address-Mr. Bouchard
addressing the students of California Institute of Technology, as reported in the New York Times of February 25, 1931, said:
Why does this magnificent applied science which saves work and makes life easier bring us so little happiness? The simple answer runs, because we have not yet learned to make sensible use of it.
I am not against progress, science or mechanical development, but we must make a very wise use of these things. I am not in antagonism to the interests of labour and of the city dwellers. Far from it; I invite them to realize as has been said authoritatively, '"not charity alone but fraternity is indeed calculated to remove the mountains of misunderstanding that all too often divide us."
In a review of a book recently written by Mr. Wallace Brett Dontham I read:
Migration of farmers to cities will go on in view of the enhanced competition of foreign agricultural producers and the effect of better machinery, but industry will not offer indefinitely increased employment either to them or to others, because the technique of production is likely to keep up its advance even at an accelerated pace. The wants of the population will lag behind productive capacity since new articles or inventions for popular consumption will not be found in sufficient number or make their way to popularity quickly enough to take up the increasing capacity of industry.
Sooner or later, and I think the sooner the better, with the ever increasing efficiency of machinery, we will have to turn to the land in order to find occupation for our unemployed. We must turn to the land not only for the benefit of those who are now unemployed in tlhe city. But before dealing with that question further I Should like to illustrate by a few examples the discrepancy that has always existed between this government's treatment of the rural population and of the urban population.
In my constituency, where my people have contributed a large share of the revenues of this country, what is happening? We have contributed all sorts of taxes. We have a few hundreds of unemployed. But are they taken care of by this government? We have three projects in view at the present time. The first is in connection with the wharf at Riviere Ouelle. For many years this wharf had been kept in good repair. It was very necessary for this constituency but it was partly destroyed by a storm. We expected that this matter would receive some consideration from the government, but it has not. On many occasions when the estimates were being considered I have reminded the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart) of the necessity

of repairing this wharf. I have written a number of letters which I shall not take the itrouble to read to-night. Notwithstanding all this, nothing was done. Under the good administration of the previous government there used to be something like $20,000 spent m my constituency. The expenditure of this money took care of the floating population of labour.
The second project is in connection with the draining of the Riviere Ouelle peat marsh. When this marsh is cleared and properly drained it will allow for the cultivation of about 5,000 acres sufficient to take care of from 25 to 30 families of unemployed. We asked the government for a little help in this connection but for some reason it was cancelled.
The third project had been approved by the provincial government and had been submitted to the consideration of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) under schedule number 34. I refer to the straightening of the roadway, the building of culverts and so on, on the highway from St. Alexandre to Fort Kent. I wrote the best letters I could to the minister and told him that I desired to meet him in order to discuss the whole matter, but nothing was done. This work would take care of practically all the unemployed in my constituency.
I have mentioned these three cases in order to illustrate my argument that while the unemployed are taken care of in the cities, not the slightest attention is given to those in the rural districts. During the last calendar year only a trifle of perhaps $2,000 was spent in my constituency. I do not want to antagonize city members, but I desire to illustrate my point. There is a continual drift of country people towards the cities. This is a social disease and in an effort to cure it our longsighted statesmen claim that there is only one remedy-back to the land. But still they are inducing the country people to come to the cities by their neglect during times of stress. There never was a time when the government would receive such overwhelming support for the building up of a practical world system as the present. If the opportunity is neglected, the failure will be so much the greater.
Instead of remedies we are given promises. The following appeared in the Evening Citizen of February 7:
Defeatism
Premier Bennett addressed the Toronto Board of Trade as a chastened leader last Monday when he said:

The Address-Mr. Reid
"I would like to promise you a spectacular move that would make you hip-hurrah-but, gentlemen, you did too much of that a few years ago, forgetting that some day the bills would have to be paid."
We did that because we believed his promise that we would have prosperity. He continues:
We cannot offer you anything spectacular- nothing but thrift and hard work.
There were many of my constituents whom I could not convince to vote for me. They believed in these wonderful promises. When they came to me, I told them frankly; "My dear people, we have a crisis and you have to be thrifty; you must save your money." They were told by the other side that if Mr. Bennett was returned to power there would be work for every one. They replied to me: "He is a wealthy man and he can tell us a trick or two about how to become wealthy ourselves."

The promise was distinctly made to us, and now he comes before the same people with statements far different. I do not doubt his sincerity; I think he was sincere, but he failed. It is not my fault, and perhaps it is not his; but his policies were not proper, and he now comes to us and says he has nothing spectacular to offer. Everything was spectacular in 1930, and now there is nothing for it but thrift and hard work. One thing however is now left out-iron heelism. May I say that we need no new Moses to lead us out of our plight. The cure is the application of common sense and the old and tried principle of freer trade and economy.
Let us consider for a moment something that goes deeper than this. As I said at the beginning, under the present administration of the world, every country is over-urbanized, over-industrialized and under-ruralized. What is the remedy? Expansion of farming. The land always remains the safe refuge. I know that it will bring a smile to the lips of industrially-minded people, and it may seem paradoxical, when the Prime Minister of the country is talking about reducing wheat acreage, to suggest as a remedy the expansion of farming. But the fact is that agriculture is Canada's fundamental industry, and when I say this I am not suggesting an increase in farm lands but an increase in the farming population of the country. I repeat, with the ever-increasing efficiency of machinery how can 74726-29
you take care not only of the unemployed of to-day but of the unemployed of the future? We have receded too fast from a civilization which was rural towards a civilization which is over-industrialized. Perhaps I might quote a paragraph or so from an article from its Dublin correspondent, under the heading, The Great Safeguard, which appeared in The London Times of January 31, 1932:
With eight persons on the land for one in manufacturing industry we have escaped the burden of direct unemployment and urban distress. The economic hardihood of the small farmer and his family has been the country's great safeguard and has enabled it so far to battle with the storm.
Let me for a moment discuss the great cry, "back to the land." The most pressing aspect of unemployment in the future will be to find occupation for the people outside large scale industry, and therefore "back to the land" is the watchword. There is at least a redeeming feature in the present crisis: people are thinking more rurally. I do not quarrel with those who advertise the back to the land movement but I doubt its success except in special cases, and I am sure that when the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Fournier) spoke about the back to the land movement he had colonization more in mind. I am strongly in favour of colonization, but the back to the land proposal is a terrible indictment of our social system.

speechtext:
In rising to make a few remarks in regard to the speech from the throne I wish to discuss some items therein affecting particularly British Columbia. The present speech, like many of its predecessors, contains some platitudes and some proposed legislation, and in the first place I wish to deal with the trade agreements. I notice that every hon. member on the other side who has spoken has taken time to put before the house figures showing that the trade with Great Britain has greatly increased under the present administration as compared with our trade heretofore. These figures are put forward in phrases that are very cleverly drawn up, because I find on page 128 of Canada 1934, an official handbook issued by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, the statement that Canada's total trade for the fiscal year 1933 amounted to over $880,000,000 a reduction of 23-9 per cent compared with 1932 and 48-5 per cent compared with 1931, but this is the sentence that interests me particularly:
In spite of the large decrease in tne past three years total trade is now nearly eight times that at confederation.

The Address-Mr. Reid

Surely that is going back pretty far for a comparison. Hon. gentlemen are endeavouring to convey to the country the impression that since the Ottawa agreements have been put into effect Canada's trade has been just wonderful. But if one examines the figures closely one must be impressed with certain facts. Granted that the trade with Great Britain has increased, why should it not increase?-because during the first two years after our hon. friends opposite came into office, that trade had greatly decreased and the trade of Canada generally had gone down to the lowest level in many years. So, if trade between Great Britain and Canada has increased, this is no wonder when you have in mind the low ebb it had reached at least prior to 1933. I would point out that our trade with Great Britain in relation to our total trade is really less than it was in 1929 when the Liberal party was in power. That is significant. In listening to speeches delivered by hon. gentlemen opposite bolstering up the trade figures, I was reminded of a man whose business in 1930 amounted to $10,000, which in 1931 had dropped to 81,000 and in 1932 had increased to $2,000. In making out his report to the directors he stated that during 1932 the business of the firm had increased 100 per cent. That is just as good an argument as telling the house and the country that Canada's trade with Great Britain has increased, because we know that it was at the lowest ebb it had reached in many a long year.
I listened to the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), both in the house and in Vancouver, giving prices of agricultural products in this country as against those across the line and elsewhere, and pointing out that we in Canada were receiving higher prices for our products than they were in the United States and, I believe, in some other countries. When he was quoting prices on certain agricultural products affecting British Columbia, particularly eggs, I noticed that when he picked out the prices and the cities in which those prices prevailed, he compared prices in Montreal, which is, by the way, a cold city, with those in Kansas City, which has, I believe, a warm climate. But he omitted to mention that in the state of Washington, which is adjacent to British Columbia, they were at the time paying two cents a dozen more than was being received in our province. If he had cited the prices prevailing in two contiguous areas with similar climatic conditions, the comparison would have been

much fairer than one based on Montreal and Kansas City.
I shall, however, mention prices of some other agricultural products in British Columbia, and I shall ask hon. members to tell me after I am through where the farmer is getting less. Just before I left for Ottawa a farmer close to me had three cows to sell. I am aware that cow meat is not the very best; we all know that prime fat steers are the best for the market. These cows ran from 1,000 to 1,200 pounds live weight, and he was offered 815 for the three. Another farmer close to me had two cows for sale when the dealer came around and he wns offered $3 for the two. I well remember the farmer's remark to the buyer; >he said: "Well, I 'have never sold a cow for $1.50 in my life before, but I will tell you what I will do; I will sell you one for S3 and give you the other for nothing." I mention this just, as the Prime Minister has often stated, to keep the record straight.
I am going to cite a case in regard to fruit and this time I shall not confine it to the Fraser valley and Vancouver. This information was given to me by a fruit grower at a place called, I believe Fauquier, while I was going through the interior during the last election. He shipped seventeen boxes of pears to Medicine Hat. I would like the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gershaw) to hear this. This man was charged $13.18 for freight, and after all charges were paid he received only $2.29 out of which he had to pay for the nails and the boxes. The result was that seventeen boxes of bartlett pears netted him exactly six cents. One does not quote these figures with any degree of pride. Why should he? Why should any hon. member come here and glory because the farmers or any other producers are getting low prices? I am mentioning these facts because we have heard so much about prices in Canada being higher than in the United States or other countries. I am citing figures on which I have the facts, and I ask hon. members to tell me where farmers have been getting for that class of product less than the prices I have mentioned.
In the legislation that we expect will be introduced by the government at this session, I am interested particularly at this time in that with regard to marketing, and I should like to spend a few moments in dealing with it. Let me say in passing that I hope the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) and the Prime Minister will expedite as much as they can the marketing legislation, particularly as it affects the milk producers of the Fraser valley. My reason for asking this is that we

The Address-Mr. Reid
in British Columbia, and particularly in the Fraser valley, are anxiously awaiting the proposed legislation because, if it is unduly delayed, it will mean that no amending legislation can be put through by the provincial government this session to enable the dairy farmers of the Fraser valley to take advantage of any dominion legislation in order to improve the present condition and prices there. For the benefit of the house I should like to give a resume of the conditions affecting milk producers in that area.
There are some 3,000 milk farmers in the Fraser valley and the lower mainland, owning approximately 45.000 cows, the yield being roughly speaking, 7,000,000 pounds of butter fat per annum. Of that amount only 3,000,000 pounds are sold in the shape of fluid milk which has been selling to the householder for nine cents a quart, the present price now being, I believe, one cent higher. The remaining 4.000,000 pounds must be sold in the form of butter, cheese, evaporated milk and other products which sell to the householder for about half the price of milk. The milk farmer is receiving two and a half cents a quart for his pool price, but Vancouver milk prices are nine cents a quart delivered at the door and eight cents at the retail stores. Of the 3,000 milk farmers, 2,700 are organized; the other 300 are independent. Some of those 300 independents underbid and thus prevent any attempt at stabilizing the price of milk, because the independents go after the fluid milk market, where the price is the best and the profits are higher, and undercut the cooperatives who must share the low returns of all milk products marketed. They also raise the cost of distribution because they duplicate services which should be unified. There are seventeen distributors delivering milk, but only a handful of farmers who are selling milk from door to door. Their wagons are peddling milk from door to door in a ruinous way and the milk farmer is paying for this duplicate distribution and for the nerve-wracking price cutting tactics of the independent. It is not the consumer that is breaking the prices. Vancouver is getting milk at 9 cents; Calgary pays 11 cents, Edmonton 10 cents, Winnipeg 10 cents and Victoria 11 cents, showing that Vancouver is not holding up the consumer in the price of milk. Instead of 30 cents a pound that the farmer is now getting for butter fat, he could be getting nearly 40 cents; instead of 2i cents per quart he could be getting 3 cents or 3i cents. By eliminating duplication in distribution the farmer could be paid still more, probably another cent per quart, and 74726-29^
the consumers in Vancouver would not be called upon to pay any more, because it is the cost of distribution that is running up the overhead. Vancouver consumers use 80,000 quarts of fluid milk per day. If the farmers could be paid two cents a quart more by the above methods, it would mean an additional $1,600 a day or well over half a million dollars a year for the farmers of the Fraser valley and the lower mainland. That is the price that 3,000 farmers are paying for the refusal of 300 independents to cooperate. We hope that the legislation that is to come will be brought down just as soon as the Minister of Agriculture and the Prime Minister can have it placed before us for consideration. It should be brought down before the session at Victoria is near prorogation, because if it is left too long it will mean that no enabling legislation can be put through the provincial house this year, with the result that over half a million dollars will be lost to the farmers of the Fraser valley.
In that connection I would like to make a few remarks about the statement of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Maiclnnis) when, speaking of the milk bill, he said- that the farmers in the Fraser Valley or in British Columbia were in just about the same position that the trade unionists were twenty-five or thirty years ago. Let me say for the benefit of the house and of the hon. member for Vancouver South, and speaking as a trade unionist with as long and as good a record as he has, that in that bill the FVaser valley milk producers jumped far ahead of any trade union movement. At one stroke they went years ahead of any trade union legislation, because, as most of us know, joining a trade union is not compulsory. Members are generally brought into a trade union by moral suasion, or perhaps during times of strike by picketing.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I would like to point out that the farmers are asking legal sanction for what the trade unionists try to enforce without legal sanction.

Not all trade unionists have

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The hon. member made his speech. I know just as much about this matter as he does, and when it comes to that I have a good record in unionism second to no one in this house. I say that without any boasting at all. Trade unions never ask the government for legislation to compel every man
The Address-Mr. Reid

to join; the farmers in British Columbia have done so, and this enabling legislation seeks that very thing. But, as many hon. members know, they ran into a snag or two in connection with indirect taxation that conflicted with the federal powers and provincial jurisdiction. This statement may interest the house, and I make it with a great deal of pride, that the marketing legislation now before the government of Great Britain, especially that relating to the marketing of milk, was based on the bill introduced into the British Columbia legislature by the farmers of the Fraser valley. We take a great deal of pride out there in the fact that British Columbia has given the old country the lead in orderly marketing. Before passing on I reiterate my previous statement, because I realize how serious conditions are among the farmers out there; I ask the Minister of Agriculture and the Prime Minister to expedite the proposed marketing legislation to the utmost of their power so that we may have enabling legislation passed in Victoria this year.
There are some other matters in the speech from the throne to which I should like now to refer. I note that it states the following in reference to the world monetary and economic conference:
The conference adjourned without dealing with many important subjects, but arrived at conclusions of especial interest and concern to Canada in respect to central banks, the gold standard, and the percentage of metallic coverage essential to the successful functioning of gold as a medium of international exchange.
I repeat what I said a few days ago in connection with gold coverage: I think the Prime Minister was derelict in his duty in not having appropriated all the gold of this country and added it to the treasury, or carried out the provisions agreed on at the imperial economic conference here by immediately reducing the metallic coverage of our currency so that further currency amounting to over $100,000,000 could be issued. I am particularly well pleased, Mr. Speaker, that Canada has seen fit, through its finance -minister, to sign the agreements, which I hope will be ratified by parliament, relating to silver. I will have more to say on that subject later on, -because as the house well knows I have a resolution asking the government to recognize silver, which I hope will come up in the near future. In passing however, I should like to say that I think great praise should be given to the United States for giving a lead in this regard, especially as they have a large accumulation of gold and could have withstood the attacks of the advocates of silver; but the United States government, even though having the

most gold of any nation, was the first to lead the way in making silver as well as gold a basis for currency.
The other day the Prime Minister corrected me in what I said about a speech delivered by him in Vancouver. In that connection I will read the statement he made and leave it to the house to say whether it could not be rightfully interpreted as meaning just what I said. Speaking of the debt of Canada, including the railway debt, he said:
Where is the spirit of our pioneers who tilled our soil and worked in our forests? Did they go to the government whenever they wanted anything?
They did not ask governments to be a wet nurse to every derelict.
Many were led to believe that the remark related to those who are destitute and on relief. It was so interpreted by many there; as a matter of fact on the following day letters appeared in the newspapers .protesting against such an insult. We hiave heard, Mr. Speaker, a great deal of praise of Canadians for their endurance during these trying times; it is a wonder the government does not give the people of Canada any reason to pay tribute to the powers of perfortnance of the government.
I would like to speak also of another part of the speech from the throne, that which relates to relief. There is a paragraph in the speech which states that the Dominion government is doing everything possible to help the provinces during these terrible times of crisis. I hope the Dominion government will do all it can to help the provinces refinance the heavy loans they have had to negotiate and at much lower rates of interest than they are called upon to pay at present. In my opinion that would be some real help indeed.
When I brought up the question of relief, however, I intended to deal with the province of British Columbia and in that particular my remarks are not going to be too critical, though I have certain suggestions to offer which I believe should be placed before the house. Before doing so, however, I would direct attention to the fact that British Columbia is carrying a heavier load than most provinces. Many reasons could be given as to why that is so; I think one in particular is that due to the fine climate we have in British Columbia many thousands of people have drifted there from other provinces, and I do not think that strictly speaking, these transients should be charged against either the municipalities or the British Columbia government. Take the case of the city of Vancouver; I have here

The Address-Mr. Reid
the number of people on relief in November last, in a statement which I obtained just before I left for Ottawa. I find that in Vancouver some 6,676 transient single men are being cared for. These men have come largely from other provinces, and the city of Vancouver should not be charged with the relief which they entail. There are some 720 transient families in that city as well, a very large number indeed. If one had time to go through the list I hold in my hand, which gives the figures for the mainland only, he would find that there are 1,058 transient families on relief in British Columbia, and that does not take into account Vancouver island or the territories in the north and elsewhere which are looked after by the provincial government. He would find also that there are 6,852 homeless single men being looked after.
The Prime Minister has made it very clear, especially since the last election, that the duty is on the municipalities first of all to take care of the unemployed and destitute, and that when the municipalities are unable to do so it becomes the duty of the province. During the election campaign of 1930 it was interpreted in the opposite way, but at all events I think it would be well if some special check were made by the Dominion government and some greater interest taken in how the relief generally is carried on throughout the entire province. I do not think it is well to have some municipalities pay a set scale of relief with no work, while other municipalities pay a certain scale with work; and others again provide work but pay only small wages. There is a great deal of dissatisfaction throughout the province because of that fact.
Let me cite one case, to show the inequalities in the granting of relief. About two months before I came here I attended a meeting of returned men. One of the major subjects discussed there was the question of a German family who had been in Canada just five years and three months and who were drawing $31 a month in relief, while their neighbours, some of them returned men who bad offered their all for this country, were being given only $9, $10 or $11 a month. You can imagine the feelings of these returned men when this German flaunted his cheque in their faces. I suppose if the Prime Minister were here he would rise in his place and say thait this is not a question for the Dominion government but that it is primarily a municipal or provincial affair and that my complaint should be taken to the province. After struggling with this question for three years, however, surely the Dominion government are not going
to adopt that stand forever; surely they are not always going to hide behind the British North America Act and say they cannot do anything. It is high time something effective was done in connection with inequalities and injustices such as this, because after all the Dominion government must have some responsibility since they are contributing large amounts Ito the various provinces.
I have another complaint which I should like to direct to the attention of the government as well. As badly as relief and the relief camps were administered by the late administration in British Columbia they did one admirable thing in connection with the purchasing of supplies. As many hon. members know, many camps have been taken over by the Department of National Defence. Before that was done, however, the camps in my constituency were purchasing their supplies from the farmers in the immediate vicinity. They bought potatoes, turnips, carrots, pork, beef and milk directly from the farmers, and they paid the current market prices. It is very noticeable, however, that since the Department of National Defence took over the camps it has been Pat Burns and Swift's who have furnished all these supplies. This has occasioned a great loss to the farmers in my constituency, and they feel that there is something wrong when the produce is bought first of all as cheaply as possible by these firms, trucked into the city of Vancouver, and then brought back out again. I think the government might well take note of a situation such as that, because that comes directly under their jurisdiction and control.
With regard to relief in British Columbia, Mr. Speaker, I should like to add that some of the municipalities are still in grave difficulties. One municipality, to which I directed the attention of the house two years ago, the municipality of Burnaby, still has 25 per cent of it population on relief. I doubt if any district in Canada has a larger proportion of its inhabitants on relief. With a population of 25,000 Burnaby has over 6,000 people on relief.
I believe that public works should foe started, and I do not believe any municipality should be allowed to give relief without some return. I also believe that the wages paid those in the camps should be increased, even if the hours or days of work should be lessened. This handing out of 20 cents a day, even with food, clothing and shelter, has broken the spirit and taken the very life out of many of those who are in the camps. The government would be well advised to put into effect some uniform system throughout
The Address-Mr. Reid

so that the same relief scale would be in force throughout the province. I believe some return by way of work should be asked for, but the men should be paid a decent wage which will permit a decent standard of living.
Two or three days ago I directed a question tc the Prime Minister with regard to the entry of cattle into Great Britain. I did so because I have listened to hon. members opposite take great praise for the amount of produce leaving this country for Great Britain. The statement contained in the article which I am about to read indicates to me a very serious situation so far as the cattle industry of this country is concerned, and it affects not only the cattle industry but our egg exports as well. I read this article to the house because I wish thereby to draw it to the attention not only of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) but also of the Prime Minister. I quote from the Vancouver Province of January 27 of this year:
Grave fears for the future of the beef industry of western Canada, which have been showing renewed life, were expressed by members of the Western Canada Livestock Union at its annual meeting in Moose Jaw, according to Jack Byers, manager of the Western Stock Growers' Association, who returned to his Calgary office this week.
Before Great Britain placed the quota on Canadian exports, limiting the quantity of beef cattle for the first three months of 1934 to the number shipped during the same period of 1933, the stock business on the prairies had developed very rapidly in the production of cattle of^ suitable type for that market, Mr. Byers said, and the future appeared brighter than for some time.
"We were hoping that Great Britain, the only market to-day for our surplus, could be built up during the coming years until the period from 1893 to 1913, when 150,000 head of cattle were shipped annualy, was approached." The major difficulties of providing facilities for ocean transport and sufficient numbers of good quality animals had been practically over' come, Mr. Byers said, with the assistance of Hon. H. H. Stevens, minister of trade and commerce, when the quota, described by Mr. Byers as a bombshell, threatened to demoralize the industry in the west. He added:
"Although we are placed in a much Jess favourable position than Ireland, our chief competitor for the English business, no attempt at bargaining by negotiation was made, with the result that while Ireland is allowed to ship 1,775 fat cattle and 5,066 store animals each week at about 84,000 head in the three-month period, Canada will be limited to 7,900 head in the same period. This limitation is imposed at a time when available ocean space has been built up to 13,000 head in three months." Stockmen were beginning to realize the seriousness of the position that would arise in the near future, Mr. Byers said, and the belief that Canada would have fewer cattle to ship this year appeared to have been swept away by the facts.
As hon. gentlemen know, the industry was given an impetus by the negotiations between [DOT]Mr. Reid.]
Canada and the United Kingdom looking to the entry of Canadian cattle into that market, and particularly so after the Ottawa agreements. The article continues:
In the first twenty days of the year 3,000 head of the 7,000 allowed for three months had been shipped, more than twice the number of last year. It appears probably that the end of February would see the quota exhausted, and the only available market for the western industry closed.
The article goes on to say that this serious condition has been drawn to the attention of the government. If the facts are as stated, it will certainly be a serious blow to the cattle industry, and the fault I find with this government is that it was not active enough in bargaining at the time Ireland and other countries were bargaining with Great Britain in connection with this very matter.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that that is all I have to say to the house at the moment, because, as I said before, I shall place before the house my views on the silver question when my motion comes up for debate.

Seventy-five per cent is

That is the way the aged people in the mari-times as well as in other parts of the country were deceived. In case there was any doubt as to the position, after the Prime Minister returned to Ottawa from the maritimes he endeavoured to make sure that the people down there did not misunderstand his views. The elections were to be held on July 28, 1930, and he addressed a letter to the people of Nova Scotia on July 12. After ridiculing the leader of the opposition and his attitude with respect to the constitution and other things, he ends his letter by saying:

Faithfully yours,
R. B. Bennett,
Leader, Liberal-Conservative party.
My hon. friend, the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) says, "We will give them seventy-five per cent."
