speechtext: To date, yes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Where is all the money he promised them in 1930?
The Liberal party passed legislation which had been sought for some time by the labouring men of this country. This legislation was for the purpose of preventing fraud with respect to union-made goods. Many concerns throughout Canada were advertising goods as union-made when in fact they were made in non-union shops. This act gave the right to labour unions to own and1 register their own labels.
Before we left office we took up with the various provinces the matter of instituting an unemployment insurance scheme. Some
IMr. Heenan.]
of the provinces were in agreement in that regard, and I am satisfied that had the Liberal party been returned to power we would not now be merely talking about unemployment insurance; we would have it in operation. For the benefit of my hon. friends in the corner, I will say that when the Liberal party is returned to power, which should not be very long, we will place in operation a workable unemployment insurance scheme. It will not be one like that which I contemplate my hon. friends opposite will bring in just five minutes before the elections, some kind of actuarial scheme which will never work in a country such as Canada.
By order in council we applied the eight hour day to all government employees who had been! working over eight hours. We applied the fair wages clause and the eight hour day to all public works and public contracts. We went as far as we understood we could go under the constitution. We took the beam out of our own eye and were leading the way. We were not like the Prime Minister who upon his return from overseas not long ago declared to all and sundry that this country could not experiment in shorter hours and higher wages; it was an exporting country. I am satisfied the Prime Minister did not voice the sentiments of the majority of the people in this country when he intimated that Canadians must work longer hours . at lower wages in order that we might be regarded as a low-paying country and thereby be able to sell our products in the markets of the world.
The Liberal government did something for the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and his friends the postal workers who had taken part in the Winnipeg strike. An injustice had been done to these men by the withholding of wages from them, and the Liberal government passed a measure to reimburse them these back wages to the extent of $100,000. It was not all that they were entitled to, but it represented a fair measure of justice. And need I remind the house that the Liberal government put upon the statute book the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, which the labouring men of this country have effectively invoked. The enaiotment of that measure has resulted in the saving of hundreds of millions of dollars without the necessity of a soldier or a policeman going in to settle any disputes. I could enumerate many more, but I think I have said enough to indicate that the Liberal govern ment did something for the labouring classes of this country.

The Address-Mr. Heenan
When we come to the amendment, if anyone wants proof of the statement it contains, that the government has lost the confidence of the people, all that has to be done is to go among the farmers and the business men of the country, to talk with men in sleeping cars, in smoking compartments, in the hotels, wherever men gather together. They will tell you. The people of the country are waiting to vote against the government, but the government has not gone out to ask for a new mandate. It is manifest that this government has lost the confidence of the people.
All you have to do is to look at the condition of farmers anywhere in Canada. Go through the country to-day and ask the very question the Prime Minister himself put to them. Ask them, " How much more money have you in your pocket to-day than you had in 1930? Let that be your answer." Well, I say, let that be their answer to-day. Take the three western provinces. Their gross revenue decreased from $843,153,000 in 1928 to $273,738,000 in 1932, or a loss from 1928 to 1932 of $569,415,000-a loss incurred since this government came into power, a government that was going to blast a way into the markets of the world for the farmers of Canada. I would refer hon. gentlemen to the memorandum submitted by the United Farmers of Ontario, taken from statistics issued by the Dominion government, showing the value of field crops in Canada. In 1928 the figure was $1,125,000,000, and in 1932 it was $416,586,000, or a loss in field crops throughout Canada of $708,417,000. Not much blasting there. Every man on the other side of the house, and many supporters of the government throughout the country, promised the farmers not only to blast a way into the markets of the world but to bring about higher prices for the things the farmers produce.
Again, the government promised the workers of Canada a higher standard of living. Well, the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) has told us something about conditions in the camps in British Columbia- he did not call them slave camps but he ought to have done so. I will coin a new name for them; I will call them distress camps, because, in northern Ontario at any rate, everyone in distress is put in these camps, and given distress wages. This government contributes thereto. It allows the Ontario government to place young Canadians, the flower of Canadian manhood, in these distress camps, paying them $5 a month with their board in the summer and $10 a
month with board in winter. The Dominion government itself, up at Lac Seul pays 2C cents a day; it does not pay the men there $5 per month because if 'they lose time through weather conditions or sickness they lose their pay for that time. That is the higher standard of living which this government promised the workers in 1930. And to carry the deceit further-because it is nothing less than deceit-this government actually counts those men as employed; it provides for them in the statistics as employed men, while the Ontario ministers are going up and down the country ashamed of it- ashamed to this extent, that in their speeches they declare specifically that these men are not employed. They say that the camps are not work camps but camps where young men without homes are placed during the winter, and further that the money given them is not wages. Well, anyone knows that it is not wages; we need not be told that. Yet this government counts these thousands of men among the employed in order to deceive the people of Canada.
Take next the railway situation. I am glad to see the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) in his place, because the railway situation can be taken in any country as the best barometer of the progress or otherwise of the community. In 1929 the number employed in the railways in Canada was 187,000, in round figures. In 1931, the first full year of the Conservative regime, it was 154,000, and in 1932 it had fallen to 132,000. This last year the number was 122,000. In other words, in round figures, there were 65,000 less employed last year than there were during the last full year of Liberal regime. And this is the direct result of the Conservative party's policy of strangling trade in Canada. What does it mean in purchasing power? In 1929 the wages paid to the railway men of Canada amounted to $290,000,000, whereas in 1933 wages to railway men amounted to $160,000,000, or a reduction of $130,000,000.
Further, this government promised "amalgamation never, competition ever", and I believe that to-day they still say there has been no amalgamation of railways in Canada. But I am one man who has stood up on the floor of this house and outside as well and declared that the railways have been amalgamated as a result of the legislation passed last session, amalgamated in everything but name. It is deceit of the worst kind to call it cooperation or anything else than amalgamation. The Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) the other day made a speech, right in Ottawa
The Address-Mr. Heenan

I believe, in which he referred to the railway question; and he is preparing now for the full amalgamation of the railways. Had one of the Liberal ministers made a speech of that kind I can imagine gentlemen now sitting on government benches rising up and saying something like this, "These gentlemen have no regard for cabinet solidarity". Hon. gentlemen opposite are making speeches in various parts of the country to please the people in those different parts; but in the house the Minister of Railways and the Prime Minister say that there is no thought of amalgamation of the railroads of Canada, while their colleague the Secretary of State the other day made a speech which was practically to the effect that the railways must be amalgamated.

speechtext: He said that under certain conditions they must be amalgamated.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, if the Conservative
government is kept in power, they are bound to be amalgamated because they are strangling Canada. Last year the bill which was passed provided for what? The formation of new companies, the stock to be equally owned by the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: And it forbids amalgamation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It provides for amalgamation all the way through, and at the end the government accepted an amendment which, had 1 had anything to do with it, would never have been placed in the bill because it means nothing; it is simply window dressing. After provision was made for amalgamation of the railroads, another clause was inserted stating: Nothing herein contained authorizes the amalgamation of the railroads of Canada, while the fact was that they were already amalgamated. The amalgamation of the railways of Canada is provided for, in everything but name,, in section 16 of the act that we passed last year. That was the most gigantic piece of deception that was ever put over white men in a white man's country. We see the surveyors all up and down the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National to-day, making surveys with a view to connecting the two lines; we see the pooling of passenger and freight trains. There is provision in the act for taking running rights over one another's road and the use of joint equipment. Not so long ago a Conservative member said in Winnipeg: "All the bill provides for is to eliminate duplication."

Well, when you eliminate duplication, what have you ? You have amalgamation; there is no use in trying to deceive ourselves any longer.

there and say that we have not any amalgamation! The railroad men who are losing their wages know that we have.

such thing, and neither does my hon. friend; he is just talking,

speechtext:
What are the excuses for
all this? Not very long ago some Ontario minister who made a trip through northern Ontario made the most ridiculous excuses that statesmen or alleged statesmen ever made in this or any other country. It was flippancy of the worst kind, but it was left to one particular gentleman to make this excuse and it is one of the worst that was made. The Hon. Howard Ferguson, the Hon. George Henry, the Hon. Mr. Finlayeon, Minister of Lands and Forests, and my hon. friend the present Minister of Railways, made a trip through northern Ontario and told the people that the reason there were so many unemployed was because of the policies of the former federal government; but this is what they say now after they have had three years to put their policies into effect:
There are people who will say to you that the troubles that we are passing through to-dlay are caused by the government of the province of Ontario, or of the Dominion of Canada. Those of you who think and read and exercise ordinary intelligence and sense know that the government of Ontario or the government of Canada have not produced the results through which we are passing, but the Great war has been the cause of it.
According to this, the war that ended fifteen years ago was the cause of it and yet three years ago this same gentleman, whose words I am now quoting as reported in the Fort Frances Times of November 2, 1933, had the

Privilege-Mr. Willis
audacity to face an intelligent audience and say in effect: "I deliberately lied to you in 1930; I deceived you and I put policies into effect that betrayed you. Now I have come around to tell you that if you had used ordinary intelligence and common sense, you might have known that I was trying to fool you in 1930."
The other day when the Liberal leader attempted to quote from a prayer, the Prime Minister said across the floor of the house that this was as near blasphemy as had ever been uttered in the house. Not so long ago the same Prime Minister went to Toronto and, speaking before, I think it was the Ministerial Association, said: "Nothing but the grace of God can save this country." Now when my hon. friends think there is an uplift, that we have turned that corner for which we have long been waiting, they are not giving God the credit; they are saying that the credit is due to the policies of the Conservative government which they represent. I do not know whether one would call that blasphemy or not, but it is just highway robbery of the worst kind, trying to steal from the higher power the credit for bringing this about.
